sentences: Three years ago, I sold my car.
At first, I was afraid I would regret it.
Today, I think it was a good decision.
In the city, having a car is expensive.
You have to pay for gas, insurance, and especially parking.
Every morning, I spent ten minutes looking for a spot.
Now, I take the bus or my bike.
When it rains, I walk with an umbrella.
It's not always pleasant, but I'm more relaxed.
Of course, without a car, some things are more difficult.
Doing big grocery shopping, for example, requires a bit of organization.
And to go away for the weekend, I rent a car or take the train.
I'm not saying that everyone should do like me.
In the countryside, a car is often necessary.
But in the city, you can very well live differently.

sentences: When I left my parents' house, I didn't know how to cook.
In the first few weeks, I mostly ate pasta and frozen pizzas.
Very quickly, I got tired of it.
Eating the same thing every day quickly becomes boring, and it wasn't very good for my health.
So I started to learn, little by little.
My grandmother gave me a few simple recipes.
At first, I made a lot of mistakes.
Once, I completely burned a cake and the kitchen smelled burnt for two days.
But little by little, I made progress.
I understood that you don't need many things to eat well: fresh vegetables, a bit of patience, and a few ideas.
Today, cooking is no longer a chore.
It has become a real pleasure, especially when I have friends over.

sentences: When we hear the word 'microbe,' we immediately think of disease.
However, the vast majority of microorganisms around us are not harmful, and many are even essential to us.
Our bodies host billions of bacteria, particularly in the intestines.
Far from harming us, they help us digest, defend against certain diseases, and stay healthy.
In recent years, scientists have been closely studying them.
They have discovered that the balance of these bacteria plays a much larger role than we previously believed.
This knowledge changes our perspective on cleanliness.
Washing remains obviously important.
But wanting to disinfect everything all the time can backfire, as it also destroys good bacteria.
Therefore, we should not be afraid of microbes in general.
The real issue is not to eliminate all of them, but to learn to live with them in a proper balance.

sentences: Last summer, my friends suggested an outing: a free outdoor concert in the big city park.
I said yes right away.
We arrived around seven o'clock to find a good spot.
The park was already full of people.
We laid our blanket on the grass.
In the meantime, we had a picnic.
Everyone had brought something: bread, cheese, fruit, a lemon cake.
Children were running everywhere, and an old man was already dancing by himself, even before the music.
The sun slowly set behind the trees.
The sky turned orange, then pink, then purple.
And when night fell, the musicians came on stage.
From the first song, I understood why people love outdoor concerts.
The music rose into the sky with the lights.
People were singing and dancing on the grass.
My best friend, who never dances, danced all evening!
During a soft song, I lay down on the blanket, the stars above me.
I thought: this is it, the happiness of summer.
The concert ended around eleven o'clock.
We walked home, our heads full of music.
This summer, the band is coming back.
This time, I'm the one bringing the lemon cake.

sentences: Modern sports have become talkative.
Apps publish our routes, clubs organize group outings, and social networks display everyone's performances.
Running has become a social activity, measured, compared, and commented on.
That's perfectly fine — for those it motivates.
But I would like to defend here the other path, mine: that of the solitary runner.
When I tell running friends that I always run alone, I often see a hint of pity in their eyes.
Poor thing, he hasn't found anyone.
That's a misunderstanding: solitude is not something I endure, it's what I seek.
Running alone is first and foremost total freedom.
I leave when I want, where I want.
If I feel good, I extend the route without asking anyone's opinion; if my legs are heavy, I slow down without apologizing.
There is no pace to follow, no conversation to maintain, no level to prove.
The group always imposes a negotiation; solitude imposes nothing.
It's also a rare moment of mental silence.
My life, like everyone else's, is saturated with demands: messages, meetings, notifications, decisions.
During an hour of running, all of that stops.
In the first few minutes, the day's thoughts still swirl.
Then, kilometer after kilometer, they settle like dust after a car passes.
What remains is the breath, the rhythm of the steps, the landscape that unfolds.
Some call this meditation.
I don't like big words: I would simply say that I hear my thoughts again.
It's actually while running that my best ideas come to me.
Problems that had been blocking me for days sometimes resolve themselves around a bend.
It's not magic: the mind, finally freed from urgency, quietly does its foundational work.
I will add a confession: running alone has reconciled me with slowness.
Without an audience, there's no need to put on a show.
Some days, I jog barely faster than a hurried walker, and that's just fine.
My watch knows my times; it has the delicacy to keep them to itself.
I'm not saying that the group doesn't have its joys — the competition, the encouragement, the post-run coffee.
I sometimes enjoy it with pleasure.
But if you've never run alone, without music, without a companion, and without a goal, try it once.
You might discover, like me, that this appointment with yourself is the most faithful of all.

sentences: Listen closely, right now.
Even in what you believe to be calm, a background noise surrounds you: the hum of a device, the distant murmur of traffic, an engine, a voice.
In a big city, complete silence hardly ever exists.
We are immersed in noise from morning to night, and often at night, to the point that we no longer hear it.
This deafness to noise may be the problem: by getting used to it, we have stopped measuring what it costs us.
However, this cost is real and documented.
Noise is not just a temporary nuisance; it is a health hazard, which health authorities now classify among the major urban pollutants.
Prolonged exposure to noise raises blood pressure, disrupts sleep even when we think we have adapted, and keeps the body in a state of constant tension.
The mechanism is ancient: our body, inherited from times when a sudden noise signaled danger, reacts to sound with a discreet but constant alert.
We no longer startle consciously, but our body remains on high alert.
Noise tires us without our knowledge.
The effect on the mind is just as profound.
Concentration requires filtering, constantly, a mass of distracting sounds, and this filtering is exhausting.
Studies show that reading, memorization, and reasoning deteriorate in a noisy environment — this is particularly evident among children educated near busy roads.
Thinking requires a certain peace; noise gnaws at our mental resources even before we begin.
That is why silence, once commonplace, has become a luxury — in almost economic terms.
Now we must pay or go far away to obtain it: hotel rooms 'in peace' sold at a higher price, retreats in remote locations, expensive noise-canceling headphones.
Silence has joined clean air and dark nights in the category of goods that were once free and are now rare.
This scarcity speaks volumes about what our development has, unwittingly, destroyed.
But we must avoid a misunderstanding.
The silence in question here is not the total absence of sound, which would be grim.
A 'silent' forest rustles with a thousand sounds — the wind, a bird, water.
Those sounds do not tire; they soothe.
What exhausts us is human noise, mechanical, incessant, and meaningless.
And the true silence sought is not just acoustic: it is an inner space, a pause in the flow of demands, where the mind can finally rest and reconnect.
We will not give up cities, nor the joyful exchange of voices, laughter, and music, which also contribute to the richness of life.
But recognizing the value of silence, giving it a place — a few minutes, a location, a moment — is not fleeing the world.
It is simply stopping the noise from deciding for us the state of our body and mind.

sentences: In just about fifteen years, a behavior unprecedented in human history has become so commonplace that we no longer notice it: publicly sharing moments of our lives.
A meal, a trip, a growing child, a morning thought — everything is photographed, commented on, and shared with dozens, hundreds, sometimes thousands of people.
This gesture, which our grandparents would have found incomprehensible, now seems completely natural to us.
Each post is, however, a small decision about our private life, a decision we now make dozens of times a week, almost without thinking.
It's worth reflecting on.
Let's acknowledge right away what is valuable about this sharing, as condemning it outright would be unfair and incorrect.

It helps maintain connections that distance would have once strained: following the life of a friend who moved abroad, watching the children of a distant cousin grow up, feeling close despite the miles.
It also offers the simple joy of sharing what we love, celebrating happiness, and finding a community around a passion.
Many draw support from it in difficult times.
That's no small thing.
But it would be wise to pause before posting, if only to become aware of two realities that habit obscures.
The first is permanence.
What we put online escapes us immediately and forever.
An image can be copied, saved, and resurfaced years later, in a context we hadn't anticipated — by an employer, by a stranger, by a grown child.
The carelessness of a moment can become a lasting trace.
We publish in the present; the internet, however, retains it for a future we know nothing about.
The second reality, even more delicate, concerns others.
Sharing a scene often means sharing people who haven't asked for it: friends in a group photo, and especially children.
A child cannot consent to having their face, moments, and clumsiness exposed to thousands of eyes and archived forever.
Deciding for them is to take control of a private life that is not ours.
This question, long ignored, is just beginning to be asked seriously, and it's uncertain whether the generation thus exposed will be grateful to us.
Should we conclude that we should hide everything, retreat into secrecy, ban all images?
Certainly not — that would be swinging from one extreme to another.
The issue is not to choose between showing everything and hiding everything, but to regain some discernment where automation reigns.
We should ask ourselves, before posting: does this really concern everyone?
Are others involved without having wanted to be?
Do I want this to still exist in ten years?
Moreover, in keeping certain moments to ourselves, there is not a lack of sincerity, but perhaps the opposite.
Not exposing everything means recognizing that a moment fully lived is enough in itself, that it doesn't need an audience to be real.
The most precious moments are sometimes those we do not share — those we are content to live.
In a world that pushes us to show everything, deciding to keep part of our life for ourselves and our loved ones is not hiding.
It's protecting what is most valuable.

sentences: In the past, a small job was often a summer job for a student.
Today, more and more adults are living solely from these small jobs.
This is called 'the gig economy.'
What is it about?
Delivering meals by bike, walking dogs, driving passengers, cleaning for individuals: these are simple tasks that are often found through an app on your phone.
There's no need to go through a long interview or send a resume: you sign up, and you start working.
The big advantage is freedom.
You don't have a boss watching every minute.
You choose your hours: you can work in the morning, in the evening, or only on weekends.
For a parent or a student, this flexibility is valuable.
You are, in a way, your own boss.
But there is a price to pay.
These jobs are often precarious: the pay is not guaranteed, and it changes from week to week.
There is no stable contract, no security in case of illness.
When you are self-employed, no one takes care of you.
The gig economy therefore raises a difficult question for the future of work.
Should we prefer freedom and flexibility, or the security of a traditional job?
The answer is not simple.
What is certain is that the world of work is changing quickly, and these small jobs are no longer so small.

sentences: There is a subject that people are less willing to talk about than politics, religion, or even their private lives: money.
Asking someone how much they earn is considered rude in many cultures.
Money is the last great taboo.
But is this silence really a good thing?
The reasons for this discomfort are old and deep.
Talking about one's salary risks being judged: if you're too rich, you seem pretentious; if you're too poor, you feel ashamed.
It also exposes you to comparison, that subtle poison that turns neighbors into rivals.
So, out of caution, people prefer to remain silent, and this discretion is passed down from generation to generation as a rule of good manners.
However, this taboo has a cost, and it doesn't always benefit those who stay silent.
In the workplace, for example, silence about salaries mainly benefits employers: when no one knows what others earn, it becomes harder to notice injustice or negotiate.
Transparency, on the other hand, allows for comparison and sometimes corrects differences that have no reason to exist.
Silence also weighs heavily in private life.
How many couples avoid the topic until the day a hidden debt or secret spending causes a real crisis?
How many families tear apart, upon the death of a loved one, for having never calmly addressed these issues?
Not talking about money doesn't make money problems disappear; it simply allows them to grow in the shadows.
Of course, it's not about flaunting your bank account at the first meeting.
But it would be healthy to be able to talk about money more freely with those who matter: your family, your partner, your close colleagues.
Bringing up the subject honestly requires a bit of courage and a lot of trust.
In return, it avoids many misunderstandings, and often many injustices.
The real taboo, in the end, may not be money itself, but the fear of what it reveals about us.

sentences: On Sundays, the whole family eats together.
It's a tradition.
There are eight people at the table.
My mother prepares lunch.
She makes chicken with potatoes.
It smells very good in the house.
I'm hungry!
At one o'clock, we sit down at the table.
My father opens a bottle of wine.
"Enjoy your meal!" he says.
First, we eat a tomato salad.
Then, there's the chicken.
It's delicious.
My grandmother eats slowly.
My little brother eats very fast.
"More chicken?" my mother asks.
"Yes, please," I reply.
After the main dish, there's cheese.
My father loves camembert.
Finally, there's dessert: a chocolate cake.
Everyone is happy.
We talk a lot at the table.
We talk about the week, work, and school.
At four o'clock, we're still there.
The meal is finished, but we stay together.
That's Sunday.
The train leaves at two forty, exactly on time.
I find my seat, next to the window.
I like window seats.
Opposite me, there is an elderly lady.
She is reading a book.
She says hello to me.
The train leaves the city.
First, I see buildings.
Then, everything changes.
Now, there are fields, cows, and small villages.
The countryside is green and calm.
I look out the window for a long time.
It's relaxing.
At four o'clock, I'm hungry.
I take out my sandwich and an apple.
The lady also takes out her meal.
"Would you like some cheese?" she asks.
"Thank you very much!"
We talk for an hour.
She is going to see her daughter and her grandchildren.
The train arrives in Bordeaux.
"Have a nice weekend!" says the lady.
"Thank you!"
"You too!"
I don't know her name.
But this trip was very pleasant.

sentences: Last Saturday, I decided to try a new recipe.

My colleague Aïcha had given me the recipe for a tajine, a Moroccan dish.
She told me, 'It's easy, but it takes time.'
First, I went grocery shopping.
I needed chicken, onions, lemons, olives, and a lot of spices.
I didn't know some of the spices.
I asked the seller, and he explained it to me well.
At home, I started at four o'clock.
I chopped the onions and cried, as always!
Then I put the chicken in a large pot with a bit of oil.
Next, I added the spices.
The kitchen smelled really good.
It was a completely new smell for me.
I added the lemons, olives, and a bit of water.
Then I lowered the heat and waited.
The dish cooked for an hour and a half.
In the meantime, I tidied up the kitchen and set the table.
When my brother arrived at seven o'clock, he said, 'Wow!
It smells so good!'
We ate the tajine with bread.
It was delicious, really.
I sent a message to Aïcha: 'Thank you!
I will make it again.'
She replied, 'Next time, come eat it at my place.'

sentences: This year, spring arrived very early.
In February, the trees in the garden already had flowers.
At first, it was beautiful.
It was eighteen degrees in the middle of February!
We had lunch outside, in t-shirts.
People were smiling in the street and the café terraces were full.
But my neighbor, who has an orchard, was not happy at all.
"It's beautiful, but it's bad," he told me.
"Way too early."
I didn't understand.
He explained it to me.
When the trees bloom, they become fragile.
If the cold comes back afterwards, the flowers die, and without flowers, there are no fruits.
"And the cold almost always comes back," he added.
He was right.
At the beginning of April, there was a frost for two nights.
In the morning, the flowers on his apricot trees were brown.
They were dead.
He lost almost all of his apricot harvest.
It was the third time in five years.
Farmers are trying solutions: candles between the trees, big fans, sometimes water.
But all of this is expensive and doesn't always work.
This summer, apricots were rare and expensive at the market.
When I saw the price, I thought about those two nights in April.

sentences: In my company, we have a medical check-up every two years.
It's mandatory, and I used to think it was pointless.
In February, it was my turn.
I went there without thinking about it, between two meetings.
The nurse first took the usual measurements: weight, height, and vision.
Then she took my blood pressure.
She noted the number, then she did it again five minutes later, without saying anything.
"Is there a problem?" I asked.
"Your blood pressure is a bit high.
It's not serious, but it's not ideal."
I was surprised.
I'm forty-two years old, I'm not in bad health, I don't smoke.
Then, the occupational doctor asked me a lot of questions.
"Do you sleep well?"
"How much coffee do you drink?"
My answers were honest: six hours of sleep, five or six coffees a day, and yes, I've been stressed for six months.
He told me: "None of this is dramatic.
But all of this together, over the years, can become a problem."
He didn't give me any medication.
He advised me to see my doctor in three months and to start with one thing: reduce coffee.
I went from six coffees to two.
Three months later, my blood pressure was normal.
Now, I no longer find this check-up pointless.

sentences: One evening in May, around ten o'clock, I heard a noise in the garden.
I took a lamp and went outside.
Under the hedge, there was a hedgehog.
It curled up right away and didn't move again.
I quickly went back inside so as not to disturb it, but I was happy.
I had never seen a hedgehog at my home.
The next day, I looked for information.
Hedgehogs are becoming increasingly rare in France.
Their numbers have decreased a lot over the past thirty years.
The reasons are many: roads, chemical products, and especially overly tidy gardens.
A hedgehog needs dead leaves and wild corners to sleep and eat.
So I changed a few habits.
First, I stopped using products against slugs.
These products also kill the animals that eat them.
And the hedgehog eats slugs: it's a free gardener.
Then, I left a corner of the garden untouched, with leaves and branches.
Finally, I made a small hole at the bottom of my fence.
This may seem strange, but hedgehogs walk one or two kilometers at night.
If all the gardens are closed, they can no longer move around.
This summer, I saw the hedgehog four times.
One evening, there were two.

sentences: A few years ago, I used to travel in a certain way: trying to see as much as possible in the least amount of time.
Five cities in seven days, three museums a day, a checklist.
I would come back exhausted, with seven hundred photos and strangely blurry memories.
I would confuse the churches.
I couldn't remember in which city I had eaten a specific dish.
For the past three years, I've been doing the opposite: spending the entire stay in just one city, or even just one neighborhood.
The change has been deeper than expected.
When you stay in the same place for several days, you stop being a rushed visitor.
You have the same coffee in the morning, and by the third day, the waitress recognizes you.
You understand the rhythm of the place: what time the streets fill up, which day is market day, where the locals actually go to eat.
You also have time for off days, which is valuable.
It's raining?
That's okay, there are still four days left.
In a tight schedule, a rainy day ruins everything.
This way of traveling has another advantage, which is less personal.
Staying longer in the same place reduces travel, thus lowering emissions related to travel, and the money spent benefits the local economy more than the transport companies.
I'm not claiming that this is the only good method.
A first trip to a country sometimes justifies moving around a lot.
But I no longer count the cities I've visited.
I count the places where I've ended up feeling a bit at home.

sentences: In France, most administrative procedures are now done online: declaring income, requesting assistance, renewing a document, making a medical appointment.
For the majority of people, this is progress: faster, available at any time, without waiting in line.
But a significant part of the population faces real difficulties.
We talk about illiteracy in digital technology, or digital exclusion.
According to estimates, several million people are affected in France.
We spontaneously imagine elderly people, and they indeed make up a significant portion.
But it would be a mistake to stop there.
There are also people who do not have suitable equipment: a smartphone does not replace a computer for filling out a complex form or uploading documents.
There are those who live in areas where the connection is still poor.
There are those who find it difficult to read administrative French — a language that is already complicated on paper and does not improve on screen.

A significant percentage of people give up rights they are entitled to, due to their inability to complete the procedure.
Solutions exist: 'France Services' in the regions, digital mediators, and maintaining physical and telephone support.
But these measures require a clear political choice: to consider that support is part of the service, and not a cost to be reduced.
An administration accessible only online is not accessible to everyone.

sentences: People often imagine that a successful relationship is one without conflict.
Research conducted on couples over several decades suggests the opposite: it's not the frequency of disagreements that distinguishes lasting relationships, but how they unfold.
Certain patterns consistently appear in relationships that deteriorate.
The first is global criticism.
There is an important difference between 'you didn't do the dishes' and 'you never do anything.'
The first statement refers to a fact; the second refers to the person, and it almost necessarily invites a defense.
The second is contempt: hurtful irony, a condescending tone, eyes rolled to the sky.
This is the most negative signal identified in this research.
The third is withdrawal: not responding, leaving the room, giving up.
This ends the argument without resolving anything, and the problem reappears unchanged.

In contrast, effective exchanges share a few characteristics: they start gently, they focus on a specific behavior, they allow each person the opportunity to acknowledge a point, and they accept pauses when the tone rises.
A frequently mentioned detail: when one of the two becomes too tense to listen, the discussion can no longer progress.
A twenty-minute interruption, announced and followed by a return, changes everything.
None of this is unique to couples.
The same principles apply among friends, colleagues, and between parents and children.
It's not the disagreement that damages relationships.
It's the way we handle it, and especially how we end it.

sentences: France spends considerable amounts each year on professional training.
There are various programs, individual rights, and funding options.
And yet, a significant proportion of employees never benefit from it.
This paradox can be explained by several obstacles, which are rarely due to a lack of desire.
The first is information.
Many people are unaware of their rights or don’t know where to start.
The administrative vocabulary doesn’t help: acronyms, platforms, files.
The second is time.
Training requires hours that must be taken from somewhere — from work, which needs the employer's agreement, or from personal life, which is difficult with children or multiple jobs.
The third is more subtle: the unequal distribution.
Training benefits managers, who are already qualified, more than less qualified employees — those whose jobs are actually the most exposed to changes.
There is also a psychological barrier.
Returning to training at forty or fifty means accepting to be a beginner, often in front of younger people.
Many give up for fear of not succeeding.
What distinguishes those who actually train?
Almost always, a concrete trigger: a targeted position, an announced mobility, a changing profession.
A training course 'for personal growth' is rarely completed; a training course with a specific goal is much more often completed.
The most common advice is therefore simple.
Do not start by looking for a training course.
Start by defining what you want to be able to do, and then search.

sentences: Health studies agree: the physical fitness of children has measurably declined over the past thirty years.
The average endurance capacity of a ten-year-old child is now significantly lower than that of previous generations.
Several causes are at play, and it would be simplistic to attribute everything to screens.
The way children get around has changed.
A significant number of children used to walk or bike to school; now, cars dominate, often for short distances.
This daily walk represented a regular, invisible but constant activity.
Outdoor free play has also decreased, due to safety concerns, urban planning, and family organization.
Schools cannot compensate for this deficit on their own.
Physical education hours amount to only a few hours a week, which is far from enough to meet the recommendations of one hour of daily activity.
Some initiatives aim to take action in ways other than just adding classes.
Some schools have implemented short activity sessions integrated into the school day.
Others organize group walks supervised by volunteer adults, allowing children to walk safely.
These programs have an advantage: they do not rely on expensive equipment or particular athletic talent.
Because there is a risk in thinking about activity only in terms of competition.
The children who are least comfortable with sports are precisely those who need it the most, and they are often the ones discouraged by evaluation the earliest.
The goal is not to train athletes.
It is to ensure that moving remains something normal in adulthood rather than a challenge.

sentences: The French and British education systems are less similar than one might think, and the differences go beyond just organization.
The first difference relates to specialization.
In France, students follow a fairly broad common curriculum until the baccalauréat: even in the science track, they study philosophy, history, and one or two languages.
In England, specialization occurs much earlier: a seventeen-year-old student may study only three subjects.
Each approach has its logic.
Early specialization allows for deeper exploration in a field; the common curriculum delays choice and maintains a shared general culture.
The second difference is assessment.
The French system traditionally grades out of twenty, with a culture where fifteen is already considered a very good grade and where twenty is almost theoretical.
The British system uses letters and levels, with different expectations.
This difference goes beyond technique.
A French student learns early on that they will not achieve perfection; some see this as a healthy demand, while others view it as a source of discouragement.
The third difference concerns the school day.
The French school day is long, with a proper lunch break and a meal served at the table.
Sports and arts activities often take place outside of school, in clubs.
In England, these activities are frequently integrated into the school.
Finally, uniforms, common across the Channel, are very rare in France.
It would be pointless to declare a winner.
Both systems produce competent students, with different intellectual habits.
What they mainly reveal are two ideas of what a school should produce.

sentences: The placebo effect is often misunderstood.
It is used as a synonym for 'false' or 'imaginary.'
The reality is more interesting.
A placebo is a treatment without an active substance: a sugar pill, a saline injection.
However, in many studies, patients who receive it report a measurable improvement.
This improvement is not a fabrication of the patient.
Real physiological changes have been observed, including the release of natural pain-relieving substances by the brain.
The effect is particularly pronounced on pain, fatigue, anxiety, and nausea — that is, on symptoms that are heavily influenced by the nervous system.
On the other hand, it has no effect on a bacterial infection or a tumor.
Several factors enhance the phenomenon: the caregiver's belief, the time spent listening, the appearance of the treatment, and even its price.
A pill presented as expensive works better than an identical pill presented as cheap.
This is precisely why clinical trials compare a drug to a placebo.
Without this comparison, it would be impossible to know whether the improvement comes from the product or the context.
There is also the opposite effect, less known: the nocebo.
Informing a patient about possible side effects increases the likelihood that they will experience them.
This phenomenon raises a difficult question for caregivers, between honest information and unintentional suggestion.
What it teaches, in any case, is important.
The relationship between a patient and their doctor is not an optional supplement of humanity.
It is part of the treatment.

sentences: In France, apprenticeship — this training that alternates between work in a company and classes — has long suffered from a negative image.
It was associated with academic failure: the path of those who "could not" pursue general studies.
This representation was largely unfair, and it is changing.
The principle of apprenticeship is old and effective.
The apprentice learns a trade by practicing it alongside professionals while following theoretical instruction.
He is paid, and the company contributes to his training.
The results in terms of job placement are often better than those of purely academic paths: a high proportion of apprentices find a job quickly, sometimes in the company that trained them.
Several European countries, notably Germany and Switzerland, have made apprenticeship a prestigious path chosen by good students, rather than a consolation prize.
The youth unemployment rate there is structurally lower.
In France, perspectives are changing.
The number of apprentices has significantly increased in recent years, including in higher education, where one can now prepare for a high-level diploma through this route.
This evolution has concrete causes: financial aid for companies, but also a weariness with a single model that values only one form of intelligence.
Because that may be the essence of the matter.
There are different types of intelligence: abstract, manual, relational.
A system that recognizes only one wastes the others.
A good plumber, a good cook, a good electrician possess complex knowledge.
The contempt that has long surrounded these trades says more about us than about them.

sentences: In a culture that values social life, spending time alone is often seen as a deficiency, or even a problem.
Someone who dines alone at a restaurant or travels without company sometimes evokes discreet pity.
This confusion deserves to be addressed, as it mixes two opposing things: imposed solitude and chosen solitude.
Imposed solitude — isolation — is truly harmful.
Not having relationships and feeling alone against one's will affects physical and mental health.
On this point, the data is solid.
Chosen solitude is something else.
It is the act of seeking, at times, to be alone.
And far from being a sign of weakness, it is a resource.
Moments of solitude allow for things that the presence of others prevents.
To think without being interrupted.
To feel what one truly feels, without adjusting it to the gaze of others.
To rest from a constant, often invisible effort: that of playing a role in society.
Creators, thinkers, and also many ordinary people know that a part of their best work, or simply their balance, depends on these moments alone.
The need for solitude varies greatly from person to person.
Some need a lot of it, others need little.
Neither is a flaw.
The contemporary problem is not an excess of solitude, but its disappearance.
Between work, family, and screens, true moments alone, without demands, have become rare.
Learning to be comfortable alone does not distance one from others.
It is often the opposite.
We have more to offer when we do not flee from silence.

sentences: Food banks and distribution associations feed millions of people in France every year.
They rely almost entirely on volunteers and donations.
Their operation is a great example of organization.
They collect unsold goods from supermarkets, agricultural surpluses, and donations from individuals, and redistribute everything to people in need.
This system prevents waste while providing vital assistance.
The work of volunteers is considerable: sorting, transporting, organizing, distributing, welcoming.
Many dedicate several days a week to it.
These associations deserve sincere admiration.
However, they raise an uncomfortable question, which their leaders are often the first to bring up.
The number of people relying on them is increasing, including working individuals.
We now see students, retirees, and employees whose income is no longer enough to feed themselves properly.
However, food aid, as valuable as it is, addresses a consequence, not a cause.
If so many people cannot feed themselves, it’s because something upstream is not working: low wages, high rents, insufficient social protection.
The risk, pointed out by some, is that the existence of these associations makes this problem more bearable, and therefore less urgent to solve.
Private generosity can, unintentionally, mask a collective failure.
This in no way undermines the usefulness of these structures, which respond to immediate and real distress.
But it reminds us of an essential distinction.
A generous society helps those who are hungry.
A just society seeks to ensure they are no longer hungry.
Both are necessary.
The first does not exempt us from the second.

sentences: The idea comes up periodically, and it is now being seriously debated: what if we worked less?
Four-day work week, reduction of working hours, voluntary slowdown — in various forms, the same question arises.
After decades of producing more and more, isn't it time to convert some of that wealth into free time rather than additional goods?
The supporters of this idea put forward solid arguments.
Productivity gains, they say, have been considerable: we produce in a few hours what used to take entire days.
However, these gains have almost always resulted in an increase in consumption, rarely in a decrease in working hours.
We could have chosen to work less; instead, we preferred to own more.
Nothing prevents us from choosing differently.
These arguments are complemented by considerations of health and ecology.
Reduced working hours would decrease exhaustion, allow for family life, engagement, and rest.
And a society that produces and consumes a little less would weigh a little less on a planet whose limits remind us of themselves.
However, the objections are not negligible.
Working less means, unless there are equivalent productivity gains, producing less and therefore, potentially, earning less.
But not everyone can afford such a decrease in income.
What appeals to those who live comfortably could worsen the situation for the less fortunate.
A reduction in working hours that is not carefully thought out could risk widening the inequalities it claims to reduce.
We must also guard against an illusion: freed-up time is not automatically happy time.
We also need to know what to do with it.
Leisure, too, is learned, and a society that can only fill its time with passive consumption would not gain much from it.
The question is therefore not whether we should work less in absolute terms, but how, for whom, and in exchange for what.
If managed well, such a change could enrich our lives.
If poorly thought out, it would only shift the problems.
Time, like money, is only valuable based on how we use it.

sentences: For a long time, we reassured ourselves by thinking that machines would only replace repetitive and physical tasks, leaving humans with the monopoly on intelligence, creativity, and judgment.
This boundary, which we believed to be solid, has begun to waver.
Programs write texts, produce images, analyze documents, and hold conversations.
Activities that we considered exclusively human are now, in part, automatable.
How can we think about this upheaval without succumbing to either panic or blindness?
We must first dismiss two equally misleading narratives.
The first predicts a catastrophe: machines will do everything, human work will disappear, and mass unemployment is inevitable.
The second promises a paradise: technology will free us from menial tasks and leave us with the best.
History suggests that reality will be more nuanced, and especially more unequal, than these opposing prophecies claim.
What we can reasonably anticipate is a profound transformation, rather than a simple disappearance of work.
Some tasks will be automated, others will emerge, and many jobs will be less eliminated than redefined.
Past experience shows that new techniques destroy jobs but create others, often unpredictably.
However, nothing guarantees that this will be painless, nor that the jobs lost and created will concern the same people.
This is where the real issue lies, often overlooked in the debate.
The problem is not so much automation itself as the way its benefits and costs will be distributed.
If productivity gains enrich a minority while others lose their jobs without prospects, technology will have worsened inequalities.
If, on the contrary, these gains are shared and supported — through training, protection, and job distribution — it can benefit the greatest number.
In other words, the consequences of artificial intelligence are not inscribed in the technology itself; they will depend on collective choices.
It is not the machine that will decide whether it liberates or impoverishes us, but the society that employs it and how it organizes its effects.
In the face of these transformations, the right attitude is neither resignation nor naive enthusiasm, but vigilance.
A powerful technology is never good or bad in itself; it all depends on what we make of it, together.

sentences: Credit is one of the great conveniences of modern life.
It allows us to acquire today what we could only afford after years of saving: a home, a car, an education.
By spreading payments over time, it makes projects accessible that would otherwise remain out of reach.
In this regard, it is a valuable tool, and it would be absurd to condemn it outright.
But this same tool, if not properly managed, can turn into a form of servitude.
The mechanism is insidious.
Borrowing means committing your future: tomorrow's income is already allocated to repaying what you've consumed today.
As long as this commitment remains measured, it is not concerning.
But when it accumulates, when repayments consume an increasing share of income, debt stops being a means and becomes a burden.
You no longer work to live, but to repay; you are no longer free in your choices, chained to deadlines you dread.
This shift is all the more dangerous because it is encouraged.
Everything in our environment pushes us to consume immediately and pay later.
Credit is offered everywhere, presented as easy, painless, almost free — until the interests, patiently accumulated, reveal their true weight.
The most vulnerable are the first victims of this ease, drawn into costly loans that worsen, rather than resolve, their difficulties.
We must therefore distinguish between two uses of debt, as different as possible.
There is chosen debt, measured, put to the service of a project that builds the future: borrowing to secure housing or education can be a reasonable investment.
And there is incurred debt, which finances immediate consumption at the expense of the future, and which gradually traps you in a spiral.
The first can liberate; the second enslaves.

Protecting oneself against bad debt requires a few simple principles: only borrow what you can repay without distress, be wary of easy and costly loans, and distinguish between momentary desire and real need.
This especially requires resisting a culture that makes debt a habit and patience a weakness.
The question is therefore not to ban credit, but to remain its master rather than its servant.
A loan for the service of a project is a tool of freedom; a debt that governs life is its opposite.
The whole difference lies in this reversal, which is better to prevent than to endure.

sentences: Every year, countless works are created — books, films, music, paintings.
Most will be forgotten within a few years; some will barely survive their author.
And a few, rare ones, will endure through the centuries, read, seen, and listened to long after the world that witnessed their birth has disappeared.
What distinguishes these enduring works, those we call 'classics'?
The answer is less obvious than it seems, and it involves both merit and chance.
We would like to believe that the works that last are simply the best, and that time carries out a fair selection, preserving only what deserves it.
This comforting idea contains a grain of truth: the works that stand the test of time often have a depth, richness, and quality of craftsmanship that set them apart.
There is something in them that is broad enough or just enough to continue to resonate with very different eras from their own.
Their survival is not without reason.
But reducing longevity to mere merit would ignore the significant role of chance and circumstances.
Many remarkable works have been lost or forgotten, not due to a lack of value, but by accident: a destroyed manuscript, a poorly defended author, an unfavorable trend.

Conversely, some works owe their survival to factors unrelated to their quality: the prestige of their author, the support of institutions, their inclusion in school curricula, or simply the luck of having been preserved.
The selection of time is not as fair as one might wish.
There is more.
What we call a 'classic' is not just a work that has lasted; it is also a work that we have collectively chosen to make last.
Each era reconsiders the legacy it receives, rediscovering forgotten works while abandoning others once thought immortal.
The canon of significant works is not fixed; it is constantly reshaped by the sensitivities, values, and struggles of each time.
What we regard as an eternal masterpiece is also the product of a judgment that could change.
This element of arbitrariness should not lead to relativism, to the idea that everything is equally valid and that longevity is purely random.
For while chance plays a large role, it does not account for everything: a work lacking quality does not last long, no matter what favor it initially enjoys.
Merit alone is not enough to ensure survival, but it is often a prerequisite.
Time does not always keep the best, but it eventually discards what has nothing to say.
Why do some works endure through time?
Through a mix of intrinsic value, favorable circumstances, and continually renewed collective choices.
Neither pure merit nor pure chance: both are intertwined.
This should make us both demanding of what we create and humble before what we judge — for we never quite know what the future will hold for us.

sentences: An idea that would have seemed absurd not long ago is gaining ground: granting rights to nature itself.
Here, a river is recognized as a legal person; there, a forest or a mountain acquires rights that can be defended in court.

What initially seems like a bizarre notion deserves to be taken seriously, as this evolution touches on a profound question: is nature merely a collection of things at our disposal, or can it be a subject with its own rights?
Our law, as it has developed, recognizes only two categories: people, who have rights, and things, which do not and can be owned and used.
Nature, in this framework, falls under the category of things: a river or a forest is property that can be disposed of.
One cannot harm them in a legal sense; one can only harm the human interests attached to them.
Recognizing rights for nature means breaking this division, acknowledging that a natural element can have value in itself, and not just for the use we make of it.
The argument in favor of this evolution is twofold.
First, it is practical: as long as nature is just a thing, its protection depends entirely on human will and easily yields to their interests.
Recognizing rights for it gives nature its own defense that cannot be so easily sacrificed.

Secondly, it is philosophical: perhaps it is time to acknowledge that nature has a value that is not reduced to its utility for us, and that treating it as merely a stock of resources is precisely at the root of our ecological disasters.
However, objections are not lacking.
It is argued that a river has no consciousness, no interests it can assert for itself, and that granting it rights would make little sense: it is always humans who would speak on its behalf.
There is also a fear of confusion between categories, a weakening of the very notion of rights through its extension.
Recognizing rights for a river, is it not a convenient fiction that poorly conceals that it is indeed human interests — ecological, cultural — that are being protected?
These objections are not without merit, but they do not resolve the issue.
After all, law has always operated through useful fictions: a company, an association are legal 'persons' without having consciousness, and no one is offended by this.
That nature is defended by humans speaking on its behalf does not fundamentally differ from how we defend the rights of a child or a being unable to defend itself.
The essential point may be less about perfect legal coherence than the change in perspective that such recognition brings about.
Whether nature has rights in the strict sense or not, the question itself is revealing.
It marks a growing dissatisfaction with a world where everything that is not human is merely exploitable matter.
Whether we respond with rights or other means, the challenge remains: to find the legal and moral forms of a relationship with nature that no longer reduces it to a thing.
And on this point, the mere emergence of the question is already, perhaps, a step forward.

sentences: As machines take on more and more tasks, a question arises: what will be left that only we, humans, can do?
If we can automate not only physical work but also an increasing share of intellectual tasks, where will the true value of human work lie tomorrow?
The uncertain answer may outline what the work of the future will look like.
For a long time, it was believed that the refuge of humanity would be intelligence, as opposed to strength.
But machines are proving increasingly capable of calculating, analyzing, and processing information better and faster than we can.
The realm of pure intellectual performance, which we thought was our exclusive domain, is shrinking.
It would therefore be unwise to base the value of human work on this ground, where machines catch up to us and often surpass us.
What distinguishes us lies elsewhere.
A first area where humans seem difficult to replace is in relationships.

Caring for a sick person, educating a child, assisting an elderly person, listening to someone in pain: these tasks require a presence, empathy, and attention to others that no machine can truly offer.
We can automate actions, but not the warmth of a human relationship.
However, these care and connection professions, often poorly recognized and underpaid, could very well be the ones whose value will appear most irreplaceable tomorrow.
A second area is that of true creation, not the mass production of content, but the invention of what did not exist, born from sensitivity, experience, and a unique perspective on the world.
Machines can recombine what exists; it is less certain that they can create in the strong sense, bringing forth novelty that comes from lived experience and inner depth.
The deepest part of art, thought, and innovation could remain a human territory.
A third area, finally, is that of judgment, especially when it involves values.

Deciding what is right, mediating between conflicting interests, assuming moral responsibility: these acts require not only processing information but also weighing, choosing, and being accountable for one's choices.
We can entrust calculations to a machine; it is more questionable, and perhaps dangerous, to entrust it with decisions that involve meaning and responsibility.
Those decisions should remain ours.
What emerges through these areas is a possible redefinition of human work around what is most intrinsic to us: relationships, creation, judgment, and care.
Far from being devalued, these dimensions could gain importance as the rest becomes automated.
It is also necessary for our societies to recognize and value them, instead of despising them as they often do.
The future of human work will depend less on what machines can do than on what we choose to hold as valuable.

sentences: There was a time when forgetting was the rule, and memory the exception.
What we did, said, or wrote faded away over time; youthful mistakes dissolved into the past; we could change, start over, escape who we had been.
This ability to forget, far from being a flaw, was a condition of human life.
However, the digital world has reversed this rule: now, everything is preserved, nothing fades away, and this memory that never forgets profoundly transforms our relationship with the past.
On the internet, indeed, traces remain.
An imprudent remark, a compromising photo, a fleeting opinion can resurface years later, intact, as if time had not passed.
What we leave online does not age, does not fade; it remains available, indexed, retrievable.
The past, once buried by forgetfulness, has become perpetually present, capable of catching up with us at any moment.
We now drag behind us a complete memory, of which we control neither the content nor the reappearances.
This permanence has profound consequences.
It makes difficult what was once natural: changing, correcting oneself, shedding one's past.
A teenager who makes a mistake, an adult who expresses an opinion one day that they will later deny, are forever tied to that moment, which forgetfulness would have erased.
They can indefinitely be confronted with who they were, denied the right to have changed.
Digital memory freezes people in their past, while life, precisely, is movement, transformation, the possibility of becoming something else.
That is why some have advocated for a 'right to be forgotten': the right, under certain conditions, to have old information about us erased, so that the past no longer weighs indefinitely.
This idea, recognized in certain legal frameworks, faces obvious difficulties: it comes into tension with freedom of information, with collective memory, with the right to know.
Where is the line between legitimate forgetting, which allows one to turn the page, and abusive erasure, which would rewrite history?
The question is delicate and does not admit a simple answer.
But whether we respond to it one way or another, the issue remains.
A society where nothing is forgotten is not necessarily more just; it can be more ruthless.
Forgetfulness had a function: it allowed for forgiveness, a second chance, reconciliation with a past one was no longer condemned to drag.
By abolishing forgetfulness, we risk abolishing these possibilities as well, and building a world where everyone would be eternally responsible for their worst moment.
The memory that never forgets is therefore not a progress without drawbacks.
It deprives us of a benefit we did not measure as long as we had it: the ability to let the past fade away, for ourselves and for others.

Learning to forget again, or at least not to hold everything against people, is perhaps one of the challenges of our time — for a humanity incapable of forgetting would also be a humanity incapable of forgiveness.

sentences: We have seen how difficult it is, in a world saturated with information, to distinguish the true from the false.
But there is an even more intimate difficulty, which does not stem from the information, but from ourselves: that of recognizing that we were wrong, and of changing our minds.
For we can have all the verification methods available, but if we are unable to admit our mistakes, they will be of no use to us.
The courage to change one's mind may be the rarest and most necessary virtue in our relationship with the truth.
Changing one's mind is seen as a weakness in our culture.
We admire consistency and firmness of convictions; we despise those who "flip-flop," who do not "know what they want."
In politics, admitting that one was wrong is almost an admission of disqualification.

This valorization of consistency has something perverse about it: it encourages us to defend our positions long after the facts have disproven them, to stubbornly hold on out of fear of appearing weak.
We confuse firmness with obstinacy, and coherence with the refusal to learn.
However, changing one's mind in light of better reasons is not a weakness; it is the opposite.

It is a sign that one prefers the truth to their own self-esteem, that one is capable of learning, that one does not hold their opinions as possessions to defend at all costs, but as revisable hypotheses.

Those who change their minds when the facts require it demonstrate a rare strength: the ability to dominate their pride, to acknowledge their faults, and to submit to what is true rather than what is convenient.
This flexibility is an achievement, not a flaw.
Why is it so difficult?
Because our opinions end up becoming part of us.
Recognizing that one was wrong means admitting a flaw, taking the risk of losing face, and questioning a part of one's identity.
We cling to our convictions as if they were possessions, and abandoning them feels like a defeat.
On top of that, there is group pressure: changing one's mind sometimes means straying from one's camp, disappointing those close to us, and becoming isolated.
It takes courage to face all of this, and it is indeed courage that is at stake.
This courage is all the more necessary today as everything pushes us toward stubbornness.
Trapped in our bubbles, surrounded by people who think like us, exposed to what reinforces our views, we are more than ever tempted to dig in our heels on our convictions.
In this context, the ability to listen to others, to recognize that they may be right, and to revise one's positions becomes an almost heroic act, and a condition for any possible debate.
Without it, there remain only entrenched camps, unable to communicate.
The courage to change one's mind is therefore at the heart of a healthy relationship with the truth.
It requires the humility to recognize that one can be wrong, the flexibility to revise one's positions, and the strength to resist pride and pressure.
Far from being a weather vane, the one who knows how to change their mind for good reasons is the one who takes the truth seriously.
In a world that values loud certainty, daring to say "I was wrong" may be one of the highest and rarest forms of lucidity.

sentences: Here is the oldest and most important of questions, the one that all others, in a way, serve: what does it mean to have a successful life?
What does it mean to live well, to lead a life that is worthwhile, one that can be said, in the end, to have been good?
Everyone asks themselves this, at least vaguely, because the answer given to it determines the direction of an entire life.
And yet, we rarely take the time to truly examine this fundamental question, as we are caught up in the tasks of existence.
The difficulty begins as soon as one tries to answer, because the possible answers are numerous and divergent.
For some, a successful life is a happy life, rich in pleasures and poor in suffering.
For others, it is a fulfilled life, where one has realized their potential, created, and left a mark.
For yet others, it is a morally good life, lived with integrity, in service to others.
Finally, for others, it is an authentic life, true to oneself, to one's choices, to one's truth.
These answers do not overlap, and one can succeed according to one while failing according to another.
This diversity could be discouraging, as if the question had no answer.
But it can be read differently: perhaps these answers each capture a part of what a successful life is, without any of them exhausting it.

Pleasure matters, but a life of empty pleasures would leave a taste of incompleteness; accomplishment matters, but success without joy or kindness would be bitter; morality matters, but virtue without any happiness would be austere; authenticity matters, but being true to a bad self would not be a success.
Perhaps a fully successful life brings together these dimensions, rather than sacrificing some for others.
One must also be wary of the answers that our time whispers to us without our having chosen them.
Our world tends to measure the success of a life by external criteria: money, status, professional success, recognition, consumption.
These criteria have a deceptive obviousness: we pursue them without ever really questioning them, as if succeeding in life meant succeeding according to those measures.
Yet nothing is less certain, and many, having reached the pinnacle of these external successes, discover that they are not enough, that they lack the essential.
Asking what a successful life is, is first about freeing oneself from ready-made answers.
There may be something more important than finding the right answer: it is to truly ask oneself the question.

For the danger is not so much in getting the answer wrong as in never reflecting, living without ever questioning what one is seeking, swept along by the current, pursuing goals that one has not chosen.
An unexamined life, said an ancient philosopher, is not worth living.
It is not that one must spend their life philosophizing; but an existence that never asks itself what it is aiming for risks missing out on itself.
These last reflections will not provide a definitive answer, for there is none that is valid for all.
But they will explore some of the big questions that lie behind the question of a successful life: happiness, meaning, the place of others, the acceptance of finitude.

Not to dictate an answer, but to help each person seek their own — for this is, at its core, a task that no one can accomplish in our place, and which gives existence, even uncertain, its gravity and its worth.

sentences: Indignation today enjoys a unique prestige.
To be indignant is seen as a virtue, a sign of an awakened conscience, a refusal of injustices; not being indignant is viewed as a form of complicity, a culpable indifference.
This valuation is not without foundation: indignation has historically been the driving force behind noble struggles, and the inability to be moved by evil is chilling.
However, we must dare to question this dominant stance, because while indignation can awaken thought, it can also, more often than one might think, replace it and dispense with it.
What characterizes indignation is its immediacy.
It is a reaction, an emotional movement that precedes judgment and often replaces it.
In the face of what triggers it, it does not question; it condemns.
Yet this speed, which gives it apparent strength, is also its weakness.
For the situations that call for judgment are most often complex, ambiguous, and filled with contradictory considerations.
Indignation, on the other hand, cuts through immediately, without examination, solely based on the emotion felt.
It offers the comfort of immediate moral certainty, where thought would require the slow work of nuance.
There is something more troubling.
Indignation provides a pleasure that is rarely admitted: the feeling of being on the right side.
To be indignant is to immediately place oneself in the camp of the just, against that of the guilty; it is to enjoy a moral superiority without having to earn it through any action.

This satisfaction is all the more intense because it costs nothing: one can be indignant at little expense, without acting, without reflecting, while still experiencing the gratifying feeling of one's own virtue.
Indignation then becomes a posture, a way of presenting oneself as a moral conscience, rather than a real commitment.
This drift is exacerbated by the mechanisms that currently organize public expression.
Digital platforms specifically reward what indignation produces: the lively reaction, the impulsive sharing, the emotion that spreads.
They turn indignation into a currency, a means of visibility, and encourage everyone to be indignant ever more loudly, ever more quickly, on ever more topics.

The result is an inflation of indignation that, far from sharpening awareness, exhausts and brutalizes it, turning debate into a competition of emotions where the most outraged wins over the most just.
Should we conclude that we should ban indignation, preferring a detached coldness?
That would be a symmetrical error.
Indignation has its place and legitimacy: it can be the first movement, healthy and necessary, by which a conscience rejects the unacceptable.
The problem is not that we are indignant, but that we stop there, that indignation replaces examination instead of preceding it.
Indignation that leads to thought, that then accepts to question, to nuance, to understand, remains fruitful; indignation that is self-sufficient sterilizes itself and sterilizes the debate.
The real issue is therefore to restore to indignation its proper function: that of an alert, not a verdict.
To feel the shock of evil, but not to be content with it; to let emotion call for reflection rather than close it off.
This requires resisting the ease of immediate judgment, the sweetness of moral certainty, the inclination to prefer the brilliance of indignation to the patience of thought.
In an era that elevates indignation to the highest virtue, claiming the right to think before condemning has paradoxically become an act of audacity.

sentences: We analyze work in terms of income, conditions, and time; we often forget what it involves at a deeper and more intimate level: the need for recognition.
Because what we seek in work, beyond salary, is also to be recognized — seen, valued, and considered important in the eyes of others.
This need, rarely named, nevertheless governs a large part of our relationship with work, and its absence explains many sufferings that a purely material examination would leave incomprehensible.
Recognition is a fundamentally human need, as real as material needs, even though it is invisible.
We only become subjects in the eyes of others: it is by being recognized by others that we acquire a sense of our own worth.
A being that no one would recognize, whose existence would be ignored by all, would experience itself as nothing.
This need to be recognized is not vanity; it is constitutive of our condition as social beings, who can only relate to themselves through their relationships with others.
And work is one of the major places where this need plays out.
Because work exposes us to the gaze of others in a particular way.
It makes us contribute to a common endeavor, producing something that will be judged, used, appreciated, or despised.

To be recognized in this context means to have one's contribution acknowledged, one's effort valued, and one's competence praised; it means to exist in the eyes of others as someone who matters, who contributes, who has a place.
This recognition nourishes self-esteem, gives meaning to work, and transforms a task into a source of pride.
Conversely, unrecognized, ignored, or despised work hurts in a way that no salary can compensate.
This is where a major suffering of contemporary work reveals itself, often invisible to purely economic analyses.

Many of those who suffer at work do not primarily suffer from their material conditions, but from a lack of recognition: the feeling that their effort is not seen, that their contribution does not matter, that they are interchangeable, reduced to an anonymous function.
This denial of recognition reaches the person at the deepest level, as it signifies that they are worth nothing in the eyes of those for whom they work.
One can better endure a hard but recognized job than an easy but despised one.
This dimension also sheds light on the fate reserved for certain professions.
There are essential jobs — caregiving, cleaning, helping the most vulnerable — that are among the least recognized, poorly paid, and socially devalued.
The denial of recognition then adds to the hardship and exacerbates the injustice: those who perform tasks that society cannot do without are the ones to whom it denies esteem.
Certain circumstances, by suddenly revealing the vital utility of these jobs, have brought this scandal to light — without the proclaimed recognition always translating into reality afterward.
Taking the need for recognition seriously transforms the way we think about work.

It is not enough to improve salaries and conditions, no matter how essential that is; work must also allow everyone to be recognized for their contribution, valued for their effort, and regarded as a person rather than a function.
An organization that crushes recognition, that makes people interchangeable and invisible, produces suffering even if it pays well.

Because a person at work does not only ask for a means to live; they ask to exist in the eyes of others — and this invisible need, if neglected, exacts revenge through a suffering that nothing material can soothe.

sentences: Freedom of expression is a fundamental principle of free societies and one of the most precious rights they have achieved.
However, as soon as we try to clarify its scope, difficulties arise.
Should we be able to say anything?
Are there words that a society has the right or the duty to prohibit?

This question deeply divides opinions, and simple answers, whether they come from advocates of unrestricted freedom or from those who impose numerous prohibitions, fail to grasp the complexity of the issue.
Let's start with what underpins freedom of expression, as it is often invoked without recalling the reasons behind it.

It is based on several justifications: the pursuit of truth, which assumes that ideas can be freely confronted; the autonomy of the individual, who has the right to form and express their opinions; and democratic functioning, which requires open debate.
These justifications are powerful, and they explain why freedom of expression deserves special protection, stronger than that of other freedoms.
It should not be restricted lightly, as each restriction touches upon these fundamental goods.
But these very justifications indicate limits.

If freedom of expression is valuable because it serves truth, autonomy, and democracy, then words that do not serve any of these goods and that harm them do not benefit from the same level of protection.

An explicit call to murder, defamation that destroys a reputation through lies, and incitement to violence against a group contribute nothing to the pursuit of truth or to democratic debate; they cause real harm without the benefits that justify freedom of expression.

Recognizing certain limits is therefore not a betrayal of the principle, but an understanding of it: freedom of expression protects the exchange of ideas, not every use of speech regardless of its effects.
However, this recognition of limits immediately opens up a peril, as it is terribly difficult to draw the line and tempting to extend it indefinitely.
Once it is accepted that certain harmful words can be prohibited, where do we draw the line?
The harmful is an elastic notion, which everyone willingly extends to what offends or disturbs them.
Under the pretext of protection, one might end up prohibiting any uncomfortable speech, any unpleasant criticism, any unorthodox idea, in the name of the harm they might cause.

The slope is real: from legitimate restriction to abusive restriction, one can empty freedom of expression of its substance, leaving only the freedom to say what does not disturb anyone — which means no freedom at all.
That is why wisdom in this matter consists of firmly holding two conflicting demands.
On one hand, recognizing that freedom of expression is not absolute, that it has justified limits when speech causes serious harm without serving the goods that underpin it.

On the other hand, being extremely wary of extending these limits, setting the bar very high, restricting only reluctantly and for compelling reasons, always keeping in mind that the remedy can be worse than the disease.

Freedom of expression must be defended even in its discomfort: it only makes sense if it also protects speech that displeases, shocks, or disturbs, because consensual speech has never needed protection.
There is therefore no simple answer to the question of whether we can say anything.

Neither the 'everything is allowed' that would deny the real harm that speech can cause, nor the 'we can no longer say anything' that would multiply prohibitions to the point of stifling debate, do justice to the complexity of the issue.
Freedom of expression is a difficult balance, always needing to be readjusted, between the protection of a fundamental good and the recognition of its limits.

This balance is not determined by a formula, but by a constantly renewed judgment, exercised with the constant concern of not sacrificing, under the pretext of protection, what makes a free society valuable: the possibility of also saying what disturbs.

sentences: There is a form of beauty that immediately pleases, effortlessly moves us, flatters our sweetest feelings — and yet, it leaves a vague discomfort in those who pay attention to it.
This is what we call kitsch: those overly sweet images, those overly touching melodies, those performances designed to draw tears, which provide emotion without paying the price.
On the opposite side stands what we call the sublime: that which seizes us, surpasses us, troubles us while also elevating us.
Reflecting on this opposition means questioning what distinguishes authentic aesthetic emotion from its counterfeit.
What constitutes kitsch?
Not the emotion it evokes, because authentic art also moves us, but the way it evokes it and the nature of that emotion.
Kitsch produces an easy, expected, prefabricated emotion; it does not show reality, but an idealized, softened image, purged of anything that might disturb.
It gives sentiment without truth, emotion without depth, a beauty that reassures instead of questioning.
Its very sweetness is suspect, as it rests on a lie: it makes us feel a pleasant emotion while hiding everything that, in reality, would resist that sweetness.
Kitsch is an emotion that lies to itself.
This is how it differs from authentic aesthetic emotion.
A true work can be overwhelming, but it does not deceive: its emotion arises from a true relationship to reality, including its difficult aspects.
It does not spare us complexity, ambiguity, or the shadowy parts; it makes us feel something real, even at the cost of discomfort.
The emotion it provides is not flattery, but revelation; it does not comfort us in our easy feelings, it opens us up to something we did not know.
That is why it leaves not the vague discomfort of kitsch, but the feeling of having touched something essential.
The sublime pushes this difference to the extreme.
It does not seek to please, but confronts us with what surpasses us: the vastness, the power, the infinite, before which we feel our smallness.
This experience blends disturbance and elevation, fear and exhilaration; it has nothing of the sweetness of kitsch, it is almost a trial.
And yet, it enlarges us, it connects us with something greater than ourselves, it pulls us away from the smallness of our ordinary concerns.
The sublime is the opposite of kitsch: where the latter diminishes us by flattering us, the former elevates us by surpassing us.
This opposition has implications that go beyond aesthetics.
For kitsch is not just an artistic category; it is a way of relating to the world, which prefers reassuring images to complex reality, easy emotions to difficult truths.
One can live in kitsch, tell oneself an idealized life, flee everything that disturbs, prefer sweet feelings to harsh truths.
Kitsch is a constant temptation, that of settling for a beautiful deceptive image rather than confronting reality in its complexity.
Resisting it, in art as in life, means rejecting the ease of prefabricated emotion to seek a truth that, even if painful, is better than a beautiful lie.
Distinguishing kitsch from the sublime, easy emotion from true emotion, is therefore not a subtlety for aesthetes.
It is learning not to settle for what flatters, to be wary of what moves too easily, to prefer what surpasses us to what reassures us.
This demanding requirement is that of true taste, which is not the ability to enjoy beautiful things, but the ability to distinguish the authentic from its counterfeit.
And this distinction, at its core, is a demand for truth: for kitsch, beneath its sweetness, is a lie, and the sublime, beneath its disturbance, is a truth.
Choosing the latter over the former means preferring, even in emotion, the true over the convenient.

sentences: We talk about 'nature' as an obvious reality: what exists independently of man, the wild world opposed to the civilized world, the order of things in contrast to human artifice.
This notion seems so natural to us that we hardly think to question it.
Yet, what we call 'nature' may be less a reality than an idea, a construct of our minds that, far from being neutral, shapes our relationship with the world in sometimes misleading ways.
Questioning this concept is not an intellectual game: it governs our very ecology.
First, let’s consider the opposition between nature and man, which structures the entire notion.
This opposition assumes that man is, in some way, outside of nature, that his productions — cities, technologies, cultures — are not natural, while the rest of living beings are.
However, this separation does not hold up well under scrutiny.
Man is a living being among others, a product of evolution like all species; his productions, however complex they may be, are the work of an animal, just as a hive is the work of a bee.
Where do we draw the line between the natural and the artificial, if the artificial is itself produced by a natural being?
The opposition, upon reflection, becomes blurred.
Next, let’s consider the idea of a 'wild' nature, untouched by human presence, which we cherish as an ideal to preserve.
This intact nature, which we dream of, exists virtually nowhere and may have never existed.
The landscapes we believe to be natural are often the product of a long interaction with humans, shaped by millennia of presence, culture, and transformation.
The forest, the countryside, the spaces we consider natural bear the marks of human action; virgin nature is a myth, a projection of our imagination more than a reality to protect.
What we want to preserve is not an original state, but a certain balance that we have learned to value.
Why is it important to recognize that 'nature' is a construct?
Because this idea, taken as a reality, distorts our ecology in two opposing ways.

On one hand, it can lead us to believe that there exists an ideal nature, a pure original state that needs to be restored, which is illusory and sometimes harmful; we can destroy real balances in the name of an idealized nature that has never existed.

On the other hand, the opposition between man and nature can make us think that we are outside of it, allowed to treat it as mere scenery, while we are part of it and destroying it means destroying ourselves.
The false idea of a separate nature simultaneously feeds a dream of impossible purity and a dangerous illusion of separation.
What should we put in place of this misleading idea?
Not to deny that there is a living world, ecosystems, balances to preserve — all of this is very real and vital.
But to abandon the opposition between man and nature, to think of man as part of a living world from which he is both derived and responsible.
Not to dream of restoring a virgin nature that has never existed, but to seek to preserve and cultivate viable balances between humanity and the rest of living beings.
Ecology does not need the myth of a pure and separate nature; it needs the awareness that we are living beings among others, whose fate is linked to that of the whole.

Saying that 'nature does not exist' is therefore not to deny the reality of the living world nor the seriousness of its destruction; it is to reject an idea that, under the guise of defending it, misunderstands it.
It is to exchange the myth of an ideal and separate nature for the more accurate and demanding recognition of a community of living beings of which we are a part.
This recognition does not give us the convenience of a simple ideal to restore; it imposes on us the more complex responsibility of inhabiting a world of which we are both members and guardians.
Renouncing 'nature' as a myth may be the condition for finally taking the living world seriously as a reality.
