sentences: The clichés about French and British cuisine are among the most enduring: on one side, the French art of living, the refinement of the table, the cult of good eating; on the other, a British cuisine that is often mocked for its rusticity.
These clichés, like all clichés, distort as much as they reveal, and the gastronomic reality of both countries is much more complex than they suggest.
But beyond the accuracy or unfairness of these images, the relationship to the table reveals something deeper: two philosophies of pleasure, time, and life.

What strikes one in the French relationship to the table is not so much the quality of the cuisine — a debatable and changing question — but the place that the meal occupies in existence and imagination.
In France, the meal is traditionally a central moment, surrounded by rituals, protected from other activities, invested with an importance that goes beyond the simple necessity of nourishment.
People take the time to eat, turning it into a cultivated pleasure, an occasion for sociability, almost an art.
This valorization reflects an implicit philosophy: one that grants a legitimate and even high place to sensory pleasure, slowness, and conviviality in a good life.
Eating is not a function to be rushed through, but a pleasure to be cultivated.
The traditional British relationship to the table is different, and it would be unfair to reduce it to a supposed culinary incapacity.

It rather reflects a different hierarchy of values, where the pleasure of the table occupies a less central place, where there may be a reluctance to make food a major concern, and where a certain reserve towards sensory pleasures, inherited from austere moral traditions, has long prevailed.

This disposition is not a lack, but an implicit choice: that of a culture which has valued other things more than the pleasure of the table, which has viewed excessive attention to food as somewhat suspect, insufficiently serious.
These two relationships reveal two philosophies of pleasure.

The French sensibility embraces sensory pleasure as a legitimate component of a good life, refuses to regard it as contemptible, even making it an art and a value; there is no shame in this tradition in enjoying the pleasures of the table, wine, and the conversation that accompanies them.

The British sensibility, marked by more austere traditions, has long maintained a more reserved relationship to sensory pleasure, viewing it as secondary, even suspect, preferring the virtues of restraint to those of enjoyment.
Thus, two moralities of pleasure are expressed in the simple relationship to a meal.
These differences are accompanied by a different relationship to time.
The French meal, long, ritualistic, and protected, assumes that one allocates time for pleasure, interrupts activity to savor, and does not subordinate everything to efficiency.

The more expedient relationship to food, long common across the Channel, reflects a greater subordination of the table to the imperatives of activity, a reluctance to dedicate a long time to what is, after all, just a need.
Here again, two philosophies of time oppose each other: one that allows for periods of pleasure removed from the useful, the other that tends to subordinate pleasure to activity.
It would be naive today to freeze these differences, as cultures interpenetrate, and the gastronomic landscape of both countries has changed significantly.

But what this contrast reveals remains enlightening: the relationship to the table is never just a matter of taste or culinary talent; it expresses a conception of the place of pleasure, time, and conviviality in a good life.
Observing the other’s relationship to the table is to question one’s own, to measure what is particular about it, to wonder what philosophy of life is expressed in it.

And one can, in this mirror, learn from the other: the sense of cultivated pleasure, or conversely, the wise reserve towards indulgences — for these two forms of wisdom, as often between these two neighbors, complement rather than exclude each other.

sentences: Modernity has made freedom its supreme value, and it has most often conceived it as the absence of constraints, limits, and hindrances.

To be free, in this view, means being able to do what one wants, without anything limiting it; the more constraints one has, the less free one is, and the ideal would be a limitless freedom, where nothing would restrict the unfolding of our desires.
This identification of freedom with unlimitedness is so widespread that it seems obvious.
However, it deserves to be questioned, for it is not certain that a freedom without any limits is truly freedom, nor that it is even possible or desirable.
Let us first consider what a freedom absolutely without limits would be.
It would be the ability to do everything one desires, without any kind of constraint.
But such freedom is a mirage, for a simple reason: our desires themselves contradict each other, and satisfying them all is impossible.
One who would follow all their desires without limit would find themselves torn, scattered, unable to accomplish anything, a slave to contradictory desires that would lead them in all directions.

The absence of any limit is not freedom, but a form of servitude: that of someone who, not limiting themselves at all, is tossed about by their impulses, unable to determine themselves, delivered to the chaos of their desires.
Limitless freedom turns into its opposite.
For true freedom perhaps paradoxically requires limits — not imposed, but chosen.

One who sets rules for themselves, who establishes priorities, who renounces certain desires to fulfill others, is freer than one who follows all their impulses; for they determine themselves, acting according to an order they have set, instead of being led by the first desire that comes along.
Freedom is not the absence of limits, but the ability to limit oneself, to choose one's constraints rather than to endure them, to govern oneself instead of being governed by one's impulses.
To give oneself a law, that is perhaps what it means to be free.
This conception, which ties freedom to self-determination rather than to unlimitedness, sheds light on a common experience.
We experience that the most fulfilled lives, the freest in a deep sense, are not those that follow all their desires, but those that have given themselves direction, commitment, and priorities.

The artist who submits to the discipline of their art, the one who commits to a cause, the one who dedicates themselves to a love or a work, limits themselves in a sense; but this chosen limit is the very place of their freedom and fulfillment.
Freedom without object, without commitment, without limits, is an empty freedom; the freedom that determines itself, that commits, that limits itself, is a full freedom.
We must guard against a misunderstanding here.
Recognizing that freedom requires chosen limits does not mean justifying endured constraints, oppression, or limits imposed from the outside.
The distinction is crucial: it is one thing to impose limits on oneself, and another to have them imposed upon you.
True freedom is not submission to external constraints, but self-determination, the ability to govern oneself.
What liberates is not the limit as such, but the limit one sets for oneself, in contrast to the limit one endures and the absence of any limit.
Freedom lies in autonomy — giving oneself one's own law — equally distant from the servitude that endures and the chaos that is not limited at all.
Questioning the identification of freedom with unlimitedness is thus to rediscover a deeper conception of freedom, as self-determination rather than as the absence of constraints.

This conception, far from weakening the value of freedom, deepens it: it shows that true freedom is not being bounded by anything, but governing oneself; not following all one's desires, but ordering them according to a choice; not the absence of limits, but the ability to set one's own.

In a modernity that often confuses freedom with the unlimitedness of desire, with the refusal of any constraint, rediscovering this conception may be necessary to prevent freedom from degrading into its opposite: for a freedom that would only be the absence of limits would not lead to fulfillment, but to dispersion, to the servitude of impulses, to the emptiness of an existence that, not determining itself to anything, would ultimately be nothing.

sentences: There is an experience that most human beings go through at some point, even if only fleetingly: that of the absurd, a feeling that arises from the clash between our need for meaning and the silence of the world.
We demand that existence has meaning, a reason, a justification; and the world does not respond to this demand.

From this divorce between our expectations and the silence of the universe arises the feeling of the absurd: not that the world is absurd in itself, nor that we are, but that their encounter, our demand for meaning colliding with a world that offers none, generates this feeling.
What to do with this experience?
Three responses present themselves, and the choice between them engages our very way of living.
The first response is resignation, or rather denial: turning away from the absurd, diving back into entertainment, activity, forgetfulness, to avoid confronting the silence of the world.
This is the most common response: we flee the absurd by distracting ourselves, immersing ourselves in the myriad activities that spare us from asking the question of meaning.
This flight is effective — it spares us the vertigo — but it comes at a cost: it is a form of inauthenticity, a refusal to face our condition, a way of living alongside the truth of our situation.
Fleeing the absurd does not resolve it, but evades it; it is buying tranquility at the cost of lucidity.

The second response is the leap, one that, refusing the absurd, takes refuge in a belief that restores meaning: religious faith, hope in an afterlife, adherence to a doctrine that asserts that existence does indeed have meaning, no matter how it may seem.

This response is more dignified than fleeing, as it confronts the question instead of evading it; but it resolves it, according to a certain analysis, by yielding, by refusing the absurd rather than assuming it, by giving oneself, through an act of faith, the meaning that the world denies.

Whether this leap is legitimate or illusory is another question, on which we have seen we cannot decide; but it consists, in any case, of overcoming the absurd by escaping it, by adhering to a meaning that is not given but believed.

The third response, the most demanding, consists of embracing the absurd without fleeing or escaping it: to look it in the face, to acknowledge the silence of the world, and nonetheless to live, not through resignation, but through a kind of revolt.
This revolt does not deny the absurd; it keeps it present, refusing both to flee from it and to resolve it with a leap.

It consists of living fully, intensely, despite the absence of given meaning, of creating meaning oneself where the world offers none, of finding in life itself, in its joys, struggles, and creations, a value that does not depend on a transcendent meaning.

To live without appeal, without guarantee, without given meaning, and yet to live fully: this is the revolt against the absurd, which makes the absence of meaning not a reason to despair, but a challenge to be met.
This third path has something paradoxical, even heroic about it.
It requires holding together the lucidity about the absurd and the affirmation of life, recognizing that nothing justifies existence and yet living it with passion.
It rejects the comfort of fleeing as well as that of belief, to inhabit the absurd with open eyes.
Its nobility lies in not hiding anything, in not buying life either through denial or illusion, but in affirming it in its nakedness, without any justification other than itself.
One who lives this way does not ask the world for a meaning it does not provide; they create their own meaning, in the very act of fully living an existence that no transcendence guarantees.

We must be careful not to consider this third path as the only legitimate one, as if faith were merely flight and flight mere cowardice; such judgments would be too hasty, and the question of the meaning of existence remains, as we have seen, open.
But the reflection on the absurd has the merit of clearly posing the alternative, and revealing what is at stake in our relationship to meaning.
Whether we flee the absurd, overcome it through faith, or embrace it through revolt, we take a position on the most fundamental question: how to live in a world that offers no given meaning?
And this position, whatever it may be, engages our way of being in the world.
The absurd is not a philosophical abstraction; it is the trial where our relationship to existence is decided, and the way we respond to it shapes, profoundly, who we are.

sentences: A flattering belief runs through our relationship with art: that it would make us better, that engaging with it would elevate us morally, that culture would soften manners and refine souls.
This seductive idea forms a significant part of the prestige of art and culture, regarded as instruments of moral elevation.
But it faces a formidable historical objection that would be dishonest to evade: experience cruelly contradicts this beautiful idea.
We must confront this contradiction, as it forces us to rethink the relationship between art and morality, between culture and goodness.
The contradiction is brutal, and the history of the last century has made it impossible to ignore.
We have seen educated men, lovers of great music, connoisseurs of art, readers of masterpieces, commit or serve the worst atrocities.
The most intimate engagement with the highest art has in no way prevented barbarity; executioners could be moved to tears by a sonata in the evening and commit horror the next day.
This overwhelming observation undermines the idea of an automatic link between culture and morality, between sensitivity to beauty and goodness.
If engaging with art made one better, how could we explain that such cultured beings could be so cruel?
We must face the facts: art does not necessarily improve those who engage with it.
How can we explain this divorce between culture and morality?
Perhaps by recognizing that aesthetic sensitivity and moral consciousness are two distinct things that can coexist without connecting.
Being sensitive to beauty, knowing how to appreciate art, experiencing refined aesthetic emotions is not the same as being good, just, or capable of compassion.
One can have one without the other; one can be a fine connoisseur and a cruel being, an art lover and an executioner.
Aesthetic emotion does not automatically transform into moral emotion; the pleasure derived from beauty does not necessarily lead to concern for others.
These are two different registers of our sensitivity, and nothing guarantees that the development of one leads to the other.
There is something more troubling.
Art can even, in a sense, divert from morality or serve as a substitute for it without real commitment.

Those who are aesthetically moved by the representation of suffering may feel exempt from truly caring about it; artistic emotion can offer a satisfaction that absolves one from action, a catharsis that calms without engaging.

One can weep at the sight of represented misfortune and remain indifferent to real misfortune; thus, art can provide the emotions of compassion without its obligations, an aesthetic good conscience that absolves one from actual goodness.
Far from leading to morality, art can offer a deceptive substitute, an emotion that is self-sufficient and does not commit one to anything.
Should we then conclude that art has no relation to morality, that it is morally neutral or indifferent?
That would be going too far and overlooking what art can, despite everything, provide.

For if it does not automatically make one better, art can nonetheless, for those who truly open themselves to it, expand sensitivity, allow one to experience other lives, other perspectives, and develop the moral imagination without which there is no genuine concern for others.
Great literature, by allowing us to enter the inner lives of other beings, can make us more attentive, more understanding, and more capable of putting ourselves in another's shoes.
Art can nourish morality; but it does not do so automatically or necessarily, and it depends on how one receives it.
The truth is therefore nuanced, and it requires us to renounce the beautiful illusion without falling into the opposite cynicism.
Art does not automatically make one better; culture does not guarantee morality; one can be cultured and cruel.
But art can, for those who open themselves to it with this disposition, nourish moral sensitivity, expand imagination, and develop the capacity for compassion.
Everything depends not on art alone, but on the encounter between art and the one who receives it, on what they make of it, and on the disposition with which they welcome it.
Art offers a possibility, not a guarantee; it can elevate, but it can also leave one indifferent, or even provide a false sense of moral satisfaction.

Renouncing the illusion that art would make us better means avoiding the confusion of culture with virtue; but it does not mean giving up the hope that art, when well received, can help make us more human.

sentences: There is a voice within us that judges our actions, that approves or condemns, that praises or torments us: moral conscience.
This inner voice is experienced by everyone; it is the very foundation of our moral life, what makes us feel right and wrong, what makes us responsible.
But what is it, really?
Where does this voice come from, what is its authority, and should we always follow it?
These questions, which touch on the foundation of moral life, are more complex than they seem, because conscience, however precious it may be, is not an infallible oracle.
What is moral conscience?

It can be described as that inner feeling that accompanies our actions with approval or disapproval, that voice that tells us, before the act, what we should do, and afterwards, whether we acted rightly or wrongly.
It manifests itself through remorse when we have acted wrongly, through satisfaction when we have acted rightly, and through a sense of duty when we hesitate.
This voice has something imperious, something irreducible: we cannot silence it at will; it imposes itself on us, it judges us against our will.
It is in this voice that our moral dignity resides, our ability to judge ourselves, to be accountable for our actions, to distinguish right from wrong.
Where does this voice come from?
The answers vary deeply.

Some have seen it as the voice of God within us, the echo of a divine law inscribed in the heart of man; others, the voice of reason, which recognizes universal principles of good; still others, the product of our education, our culture, and the rules internalized since childhood; and finally, some see it as a disposition shaped by our social nature, our capacity for empathy, and our need to live with others.
These explanations are not necessarily mutually exclusive, and it is difficult to decide between them.

But their very diversity raises a difficulty: if conscience is partly the product of our education and culture, then it is not an infallible and universal voice, but a particular formation that can vary, make mistakes, and reflect the prejudices of its environment.
This difficulty is crucial, as it calls into question the authority of conscience.
Should we always follow our conscience?
One might be tempted to answer yes: acting against one's conscience, isn't that betraying oneself, doing what one believes to be wrong?
There is a truth in this answer: no one should act against what they firmly believe to be good, and following one's conscience is a requirement of moral integrity.
But there is also a danger: for conscience can be mistaken, poorly formed, reflect prejudices, and approve what is actually condemnable.
History is full of crimes committed in good conscience, by individuals convinced they were doing right, whose conscience, shaped by a distorted culture, ideology, or education, approved of horror.
Thus, following one's conscience does not guarantee acting rightly if that conscience is poorly formed.
From this follows an essential requirement: conscience must be enlightened, formed, educated.
It is not enough to follow one's conscience; it must also be right, informed, and capable of judging accurately.
A blind, poorly formed conscience filled with prejudices can lead to the worst acts while giving the feeling of acting rightly.
That is why moral life consists not only in following one's conscience, but also in forming it, enlightening it, examining it, and confronting it with reflection, discussion, and other viewpoints.
Conscience is not an oracle to be consulted; it is a faculty that must be cultivated, educated, and subjected to examination so that it judges accurately.
Following an unenlightened conscience can be as dangerous as not following one's conscience.
Thus, moral conscience occupies a place that is both central and paradoxical in moral life.
Central, because it is the locus of our responsibility, through which we judge and are accountable for our actions; no one should act against it, and its voice deserves respect and attention.
Paradoxical, because it is not infallible, can be mistaken, and must be formed and enlightened.

Moral wisdom consists in holding both: respecting one's conscience, not acting against what one firmly believes to be good, but also working to enlighten it, subjecting it to examination, and not treating it as an infallible oracle.

Listening to one's conscience and educating it, following it and examining it: this is the dual duty that makes moral life not mere obedience to a voice, but a demanding dialogue with a conscience that must be continually formed to be worthy of being followed.

sentences: My best friend is named Yanis.
We have known each other since we were six years old.
On the first day of school, he sat next to me.
He gives me a red pencil.
And there you go, we are friends.
Yanis is different from me.
He is tall, I am short.
He talks a lot, I am shy.
He loves football, I prefer video games.
But we laugh at the same things.
After school, we often go to his house.
His mother always prepares something to eat.
"You are too thin!
Eat!" she says.
On weekends, we walk around the city and talk about everything.
Yanis no longer lives in my neighborhood.
His family is moving, twenty minutes by bus.
At first, it's difficult.
But we often call each other.
And on Saturdays, he always comes.
There are things that I don't tell anyone.
Except Yanis.
That's what a best friend is: someone who knows everything about you and stays.

sentences: At the end of this meditation on the fragility of civilization, its threats, the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom, a decisive question arises: should we despair?
If civilization is fragile, if evil can resurface in every person, if our powers exceed our wisdom, if transmission is threatened, how can we avoid succumbing to discouragement?
And yet, to despair would be to give up, to throw in the towel, to let the worst happen.
Therefore, we need something other than despair; but what?
Perhaps hope — provided we carefully distinguish it from optimism, with which it is often confused, and from which it differs profoundly.
Optimism is the belief that things will turn out well, that the future will be better, that progress will prevail, that everything will eventually work out.
It is a forecast about the future, a confidence in a favorable outcome.
But this optimism is fragile, for nothing guarantees that it is correct; the future can contradict its forecasts, the worst can happen, and then optimism collapses, giving way to despair.
Moreover, optimism is demobilizing: if one believes that everything will be fine anyway, why act, why struggle?
Confidence in a guaranteed favorable outcome dispenses with the effort that would make it possible.
Paradoxically, optimism can lead to passivity, making one believe that good will come about without us.
Hope is something entirely different.
It is not a prediction about the future, a belief that everything will turn out well; it does not have that certainty.
Hope knows that the future is uncertain, that the worst is possible, that nothing is guaranteed; it does not delude itself into thinking a favorable outcome is assured.
But, knowing this, it continues to act, to fight, to work for the best, not because it is sure of succeeding, but because the best is possible, and it is worth striving for even without guarantees.
Hope is a disposition to act for good in uncertainty, a bet on what is possible that does not depend on the certainty of success.
It does not assert that everything will be fine; it asserts that the good is worth pursuing, whatever happens.
This distinction is crucial, as it establishes an attitude that neither optimism nor despair allows.

The desperate do nothing, because they believe everything is lost; the optimist does nothing either, because they believe everything is already won; only hope acts, because it knows that nothing is set in stone, that the future depends on what we do, and that alone is a reason to act.
Hope is not based on a prediction, but on a possibility and a value: the best is possible, and it is worth working towards.
This disposition withstands the contradiction of facts, as it does not rest on a prediction that facts could refute, but on a commitment that nothing can invalidate.
Even if the worst were to happen, it would have been worth fighting for the best; hope is not disappointed by failure, because it was not based on the certainty of success.
Hope, as understood here, does not ignore the fragility of civilization, the threats it faces, or the imbalance that puts us at risk.
It confronts all of this directly, without indulging in optimistic illusions.

But it draws not despair from this, but rather commitment: since nothing is certain, since the future depends on us, since the best is possible although not guaranteed, it is worth acting, fighting, watching over what is fragile, defending it, and passing it on.
Hope is this disposition to do what depends on us, without offloading responsibility onto a providence that would do good in our place, nor giving up in the face of uncertainty about the outcome.
It is at once the opposite of lazy optimism and demobilizing despair: an active lucidity that acts precisely because it knows that nothing is assured.
Thus, hope, distinguished from optimism, is the disposition that suits our condition and our time.

In the face of the fragility of civilization, it does not console itself with an optimism that believes in guaranteed good, nor does it yield to a despair that thinks everything is lost; it recognizes uncertainty and acts nonetheless, because the best is possible and worth it.

This hope is not a feeling, a mood, a prediction; it is a choice, a will, almost a virtue — the disposition to do good in uncertainty, to watch over what is fragile without a guarantee of success, to pass on what could be lost by betting that it is worth saving.

It is this hope, and not optimism, that can ground action in the face of the threats of our time; for it does not depend on the certainty that we will win, but on the conviction that the fight is worth waging — and this conviction, no future, however dark, can contradict.

sentences: We talk about wisdom, we admire the wise, we aspire to become wise; and yet, if we were asked what wisdom is, we would struggle to define it.
Is it knowledge, a sum of knowledge?
A virtue, a moral quality?
An art of living, a way of being?
Wisdom eludes simple definitions, and this very difficulty is revealing, as it relates to the particular nature of what we are trying to grasp.
At the threshold of this final section, which crowns an entire journey, it is worth probing what this wisdom is that we, obscurely, aspire to.
Wisdom is not primarily knowledge, an accumulation of knowledge.
One can know a lot without being wise, be learned yet foolish; and one can be wise with little knowledge, a wisdom that is not based on erudition.
Wisdom is not science; it belongs to a different order.

Certainly, it implies a form of knowledge — self-knowledge, knowledge of life, knowledge of what matters — but this knowledge is not an accumulation of facts; it is understanding, clarity, discernment that cannot be measured by the quantity of what one knows.
The wise person is not necessarily the most learned; they are the one who has understood something essential about life and about themselves.
Wisdom is not merely a moral virtue, a sum of qualities.
Certainly, it includes virtues — moderation, courage, justice, self-control — but it is not just their simple addition.

Rather, it is what organizes them, guides them, gives them their proper measure; it is the discernment that knows, in each situation, what is appropriate to do, how to apply the virtues, how to reconcile them when they seem to oppose each other.
Wisdom is less a virtue among others than the supreme virtue, the one that governs the others, the discernment that knows how to live.
It is this quality of practical judgment that, beyond specific rules and virtues, knows what is appropriate in the concrete of existence.
Wisdom is perhaps above all an art of living, a way of being in the world and with oneself.

The wise person is recognized less by what they know or assert than by their way of living: their serenity, their moderation, their proper relationship with things and beings, their ability to endure trials without being crushed, to enjoy goods without being enslaved by them, to accept what they cannot change and to change what they can.
Wisdom is this way of inhabiting existence, this art of living that makes a life successful not by its external achievements, but by the quality of its relationship with the world.
The wise person is not the one who has an answer for everything, but the one who lives well, with accuracy and serenity, the condition that is theirs.
What brings these dimensions together — knowledge, virtue, the art of living — is perhaps that wisdom is an integration, a unity between what we understand, what we are, and what we do.

The wise person is not someone who knows what is good without doing it, nor someone who does good without understanding it, nor someone who lives well by chance; it is the one in whom understanding, virtue, and action are in harmony, where knowledge becomes a way of being, where virtue becomes life, and where thought becomes existence.
Wisdom is this coherence between thought and life, this unity of being that makes the wise person live what they understand and understand what they live.
It is the fulfillment of a life that has aligned what it knows, what it wants, and what it does.
This conception of wisdom sheds light on the entire journey that preceded it.

For all the reflections we have conducted — on time, death, love, evil, truth, beauty — were not only aimed at knowing, at accumulating knowledge; they aimed at a comprehension that becomes a way of living, a knowledge that turns into wisdom.
To understand the value of time in order to live it better; to understand death in order to live better; to understand love, evil, truth, not to have theories about them, but to live more justly.
Wisdom is the goal toward which all true thought strives: not knowledge for the sake of knowledge, but understanding that transforms life, clarity that becomes the art of living.
And it is this wisdom, more than any knowledge, that may be the true aim of all learning — to learn not only to know, but to live.

They play in the park, near his home.
Julien is in a team.
His team is called 'The Lions.'
They play well together.
On Wednesdays, Julien runs.
He runs in the park in the morning, before work.
Running is not easy for him.
But he likes it.
He feels good afterwards.

It's a real match!

They train for an hour.
Julien loves his team.

sentences: Every year, my whole family gets together for Christmas at my parents' house.
There are fifteen people in total: my parents, my brothers and sisters, their children, and me.
On the evening of December twenty-fourth, we decorate the tree together.

sentences: I have a list of songs that I only listen to when I'm alone in my car.
They're not exactly songs I'm ashamed of, but they don't match the image I want to project.
Songs that are too sentimental, too popular, considered "uninteresting" by my friends who know about music.
For years, I hid these tastes, preferring to mention more "serious" artists when asked what I was listening to.
One day, a friend accidentally discovered this list on my phone.
Instead of making fun of me, she admitted to having exactly the same kind of secret list, with equally "shameful" songs.
We laughed about this shared discovery.
Why hide such a simple pleasure?
No one would really judge us for that, or at least, not as much as we imagine.
Since that conversation, I've been a bit more open about these "popular" musical tastes.
I think many people experience the same thing: a gap between what they actually listen to and what they claim to listen to, out of fear of judgment.
My children, on the other hand, have never experienced this kind of embarrassment.
They listen out loud to what they like, without filtering based on the image it projects.
Perhaps a generation used to personalized streaming platforms naturally develops a more free relationship with its own tastes than mine ever had.
Maybe true musical enjoyment begins when we stop choosing our music based on how others perceive it.

sentences: As I scroll through my news feed, I often find myself comparing my life to that of others.
This colleague who is traveling to a beautiful place.
This former classmate who just bought a house.
This acquaintance who seems to have a much richer social life than mine.
Rationally, I know that these comparisons don't mean much.
I don't know the struggles of these people, their doubts, their own dissatisfaction.
Yet, emotionally, these comparisons affect me, sometimes more than I would like to admit.
After spending time on these apps, I sometimes feel vaguely dissatisfied with my own existence, for no specific reason.
Researchers studying this phenomenon explain that our brains haven't evolved to compare ourselves to thousands of people at once, as these platforms allow today.
In the past, we mainly compared ourselves to our immediate surroundings, a much smaller circle.
This explanation reassures me a bit, without completely solving the problem.
I continue to feel these comparisons, even knowing their origin.
Since then, I occasionally post a less perfect moment from my own life, partly to balance out this overly polished collective image.
Several followers have thanked me for this honesty, which suggests that others also feel relieved to see a life that isn't uniformly successful.
I try, when I notice this feeling of dissatisfaction, to consciously remind myself that I only see a carefully chosen fragment of other people's lives, and not their complete reality.

sentences: Since remote work has become widespread, the downtown area of my city looks different during the week.
On Tuesdays and Thursdays, days when many people still go to the office, the streets in the business district are lively, almost like before.
On Mondays and Fridays, however, the same streets seem strangely quiet.
Several restaurants that mainly relied on office workers have had to close due to a lack of sufficient customers on those days.
This recent transformation raises broader questions about the future of our downtown areas.
Some urban planners see it as an opportunity: to convert old empty offices into housing, bringing life back to these neighborhoods in ways other than just work.
Others are worried about the economic consequences for all the businesses that depended on the daily presence of workers.
In public transport as well, ridership has changed its rhythm, with less pronounced peaks during traditional rush hours.
While walking recently in that same neighborhood on a Monday, I noticed that some businesses were starting to adapt by offering services aimed at residents rather than just office workers.
This still uncertain reinvention perhaps illustrates our cities' ability to transform rather than simply decline.
I often wonder what our cities will look like in ten years if this trend continues to take hold.
Perhaps we will see reinvented downtowns, less focused solely on office work, and more blending housing, shops, and leisure.
One thing seems certain: the way we work continues to reshape, quietly but profoundly, the very space of our cities.

sentences: The debate over school uniforms regularly resurfaces in several countries, often framed as a purely practical issue: simplifying the choice of clothes in the morning, reducing tensions related to luxury brands among students, and making life easier for families with modest incomes.
Yet behind this apparent simplicity lies a much deeper question: the role of the school in shaping, or limiting, the individual identity of young people.

Supporters of uniforms put forward a fairly convincing argument for equality: without visible clothing distinctions, economic inequalities among students would become less immediately noticeable, thereby reducing certain forms of early social discrimination, even before more difficult-to-correct differences set in.

Opponents counter that this imposed equality remains largely superficial, since the real inequalities among students—housing, access to culture, family support—persist well beyond the mere clothing worn in class.

According to them, the uniform would mask the problem without solving it, while also eliminating a legitimate space for personal expression at an age when identity is precisely constructed through such choices.

This tension ultimately reveals a more fundamental disagreement about the very mission of the school: should it prioritize a facade of equality, even if it means standardizing certain aspects of individual expression, or accept visible diversity, at the risk of making some existing social inequalities more glaring?
Neither position seems to gain total support, which likely explains why this seemingly trivial debate continues to so persistently divide opinions.

sentences: Researchers who study laughter agree on one point: it is a social behavior that is much more complex than it seems, far from being just a mechanical reaction to a successful joke.

Studies in social psychology have shown that the vast majority of daily laughter does not occur in response to an explicit joke, but rather during ordinary conversations, as a social signal intended to strengthen a bond, ease tension, or signify shared complicity.

This social dimension of laughter would explain why people considered socially skilled generally laugh more and in a way that is more contextually appropriate than those who struggle with relationships.
Laughter thus functions as a true tool for social navigation, allowing for real-time adjustments to the tone of an exchange.

Even more surprisingly, researchers have observed that spontaneously producing humor suited to a situation requires sophisticated cognitive abilities: understanding the expectations of one's interlocutor, anticipating their likely reaction, and choosing the right moment to introduce a comedic remark.
This complexity would explain, according to some studies, a correlation observed between a developed sense of humor and certain forms of social and emotional intelligence.

This perspective invites us to reconsider humor not as a mere superficial entertainment, but as a full-fledged social skill, revealing an individual's ability to finely perceive the relational dynamics around them and to adapt appropriately and accurately.

sentences: Captain Nemo was looking at me.
I didn't ask him anything, but he guessed my thoughts and answered the questions I was eager to ask him.
"Most of these dishes are unknown to you," he said to me.
However, you can consume them without fear.
They are healthy and nourishing.
For a long time, I have given up the food of the land, and I am no worse for it.
My crew, who are strong, do not eat any differently than I do.
-- So, I said, all this food comes from the sea?
Yes, professor, the sea provides for all my needs.
Sometimes, I drag my nets, and I pull them in, ready to break.
At times, I go hunting in this element that seems inaccessible to man, and I force the game that lies in my underwater forests.
My herds, like those of the old shepherd of Neptune, graze fearlessly in the vast meadows of the Ocean.
I have a large property there that I cultivate myself and which is always sown by the hand of the Creator of all things.
I looked at Captain Nemo with some astonishment, and I replied to him:

I perfectly understand, sir, that your nets provide excellent fish for your table; I understand less that you pursue aquatic game in your underwater forests; but I do not understand at all how a piece of meat, no matter how small, appears on your menu.
Also, sir, Captain Nemo replied to me, I never use the flesh of land animals.
However, I said, pointing to a dish where a few slices of fillet still remained.

sentences: The doctor maintained a constant altitude that varied between two hundred and five hundred feet.
Kennedy often fired his rifle.

Above the islands, the travelers even approached recklessly, scanning the thickets, bushes, and undergrowth, everywhere that some shade or rock crevice might have provided shelter for their companion.
They descended near the long canoes that were traversing the lake.
The fishermen, at the sight of them, rushed into the water and returned to their island with the least concealed signs of fear.
"We see nothing," said Kennedy after two hours of searching.
"Let's wait, Dick, and not lose heart; we must not be far from the site of the accident."
At eleven o'clock, the Victoria had advanced ninety miles; it then encountered a new current that, at almost a right angle, pushed it eastward for about sixty miles.
It hovered above a very large and densely populated island that the doctor thought must be Farram, where the capital of the Biddiomahs is located.
He expected to see Joe emerge from every bush, escaping and calling out.

If he had been free, he would have been taken without difficulty; as a prisoner, by repeating the maneuver used for the missionary, he would have soon rejoined his friends; but nothing appeared, nothing moved!
It was enough to drive one to despair.
The Victoria arrived at two-thirty in sight of Tangalia, a village located on the eastern bank of Chad, which marked the furthest point reached by Denham during his exploration.
The doctor became worried about this persistent direction of the wind.
He felt himself being pushed eastward, driven into the heart of Africa, towards endless deserts.

sentences: Around March 20th, the hunters reported the first swans, which were migrating from the southern territories and flying north while making sharp whistles.
A few 'snow buntings' and 'wintering hawks' also made their appearance.
But a vast white layer still covered the ground, and the sun could not melt the solid surface of the sea and the lake.
The thaw did not occur until the first days of April.
The breaking of the ice happened with extraordinary noise, sometimes comparable to artillery fire.
Sudden changes occurred in the pack ice.
More than one iceberg, damaged by the impacts and eroded at its base, toppled with a terrible noise due to the shifting of its center of gravity.
This led to collapses that accelerated the breaking of the icefield.
At that time, the average temperature was thirty-two degrees above zero (0° Celsius).
Thus, the first ice along the shore quickly began to dissolve, and the pack ice, driven by polar currents, gradually receded into the mists of the horizon.
By April 15th, the sea was free, and certainly a ship coming from the Pacific Ocean, through the Bering Strait, after following the American coast, could have landed at Cape Bathurst.
At the same time as the Arctic Ocean, Lake Barnett freed itself from its icy shell, much to the delight of the thousands of ducks and other waterfowl that thronged its shores.
But, as Lieutenant Hobson had predicted, the perimeter of the lake had been altered by the new slope of the land.
The section of the shore that stretched out in front of the fort's enclosure, bordered to the east by wooded hills, widened considerably.
Jasper Hobson estimated the retreat of the lake's waters on its eastern shore to be one hundred and fifty paces.
Conversely, these waters must have moved equally to the west, flooding the land unless some natural barrier contained them.

sentences: It's true, I replied, your ship is ahead of its time by a century, perhaps even several.
What a shame that such a secret must die with its inventor!
Captain Nemo did not answer me.
After a few minutes of silence:
"You were talking to me," he said, "about the opinion of ancient historians on the dangers posed by navigation in the Red Sea?"
"It's true," I replied, "but weren't their fears exaggerated?"
Yes and no, Monsieur Aronnax, Captain Nemo replied to me, who seemed to have a deep understanding of 'his Red Sea.'
What is no longer dangerous for a modern ship, well-rigged, solidly built, and master of its course thanks to obedient steam, posed all sorts of dangers to ancient vessels.
One must imagine those early navigators venturing out on boats made of planks sewn together with palm fiber, caulked with crushed resin and coated with seal oil.
They didn't even have instruments to determine their direction, and they navigated by estimation amid currents they barely knew.
Under these conditions, shipwrecks were and must have been numerous.
But in our time, the steamers that operate between Suez and the South Seas have nothing to fear from the tempests of this gulf, despite the opposing monsoons.

Their captains and passengers do not prepare for departure with propitiatory sacrifices, and upon their return, they no longer go, adorned with garlands and golden ribbons, to thank the gods in the nearby temple.
I agree, I said, and steam seems to have killed gratitude in the hearts of sailors.
But Captain, since you seem to have specifically studied this sea, can you tell me the origin of its name?
There are, Monsieur Aronnax, many explanations on this subject.
Would you like to know the opinion of a chronicler from the 14th century?
Certainly.
This fantasist claims that his name was given to him after the passage of the Israelites, when the Pharaoh perished in the waves that closed in at the voice of Moses:
As a sign of this wonder, the sea became red and crimson.
And they could not name it otherwise than the Red Sea.
-- A poet's explanation, Captain Nemo, I replied, but I cannot be satisfied with that.
So I will ask you for your personal opinion.

sentences: However, what he had not been able to write to Albert, since the events we are about to recount occurred after his messenger's departure, is that on the same day, in the House of Peers, a great agitation had arisen and was prevailing among the groups that are usually so calm in the upper assembly.

Everyone had arrived almost before the hour and was discussing the sinister event that was about to capture public attention and focus it on one of the most well-known members of the illustrious body.
There were low readings of the article, comments, and exchanges of memories that further clarified the facts.
The Count of Morcerf was not liked among his colleagues.
Like all upstarts, he had been forced, to maintain his rank, to exhibit an excess of arrogance.
The great aristocrats laughed at him; the talented rejected him; the pure glories instinctively despised him.
The Count was at that unfortunate extreme of being a scapegoat.
Once designated by the finger of the Lord for sacrifice, everyone was preparing to cry out against him.
Alone, the Count of Morcerf knew nothing.
He did not receive the newspaper where the defamatory news was published, and had spent the morning writing letters and trying out a horse.

He arrived, therefore, at his usual hour, head held high, proud eye, insolent gait, got out of the carriage, passed through the corridors, and entered the hall, without noticing the hesitations of the ushers and the half-salutes of his colleagues.
When Morcerf entered, the session had already been open for more than half an hour.

Although the count, as we mentioned, was unaware of everything that had happened, his demeanor and gait appeared to everyone more arrogant than usual, and his presence on this occasion seemed so aggressive to this assembly, jealous of his honor, that everyone saw it as inappropriate, many as a provocation, and some as an insult.
It was clear that the entire Chamber was eager to start the debate.
The accusatory newspaper was visible in everyone's hands; however, as always, each person hesitated to take on the responsibility for the attack.
Finally, one of the honorable peers, a declared enemy of Count de Morcerf, ascended to the podium with a solemnity that indicated the awaited moment had arrived.

sentences: An old castle bathes the base of its towers in a large, sad pond, sad, with flocks of wild birds.
A river flows from there that the small boats can navigate up to the town.

And in the narrow streets with antique houses, the men wear tall hats, embroidered vests, and four layered jackets: the first, as big as a hand, covering at most the shoulder blades, and the last stopping just above the seat of their trousers.

The girls, tall, beautiful, fresh, have their chests compressed in a wool vest that acts like armor, constraining them, not even allowing their powerful and tormented bosoms to be guessed; and they are styled in a strange way: at the temples, two colored embroidered plates frame the face, tightening the hair that falls in a cascade behind the head, then rising to be compacted at the top of the skull under a peculiar bonnet, often made of gold or silver fabric.

The maid at our inn was no more than eighteen, with all-blue eyes, a pale blue pierced by two small black dots of the pupil; and her short, tightly packed teeth, which she constantly showed while laughing, seemed made to crush granite.
She didn't know a word of French, speaking only Breton, like most of her compatriots.
Now, my friend was not getting any better, and although no illness had declared itself, the doctor forbade him to leave yet, ordering complete rest.
So I spent my days near him, and the little maid constantly came in, bringing either my dinner or some herbal tea.
I teased her a bit, which seemed to amuse her, but we didn't talk, of course, since we didn't understand each other.
Now, one night, as I had stayed very late beside the sick man, I crossed paths, on my way back to my room, with the girl who was returning to hers.

It was right in front of my open door; then, suddenly, without thinking about what I was doing, more as a joke than anything else, I grabbed her by the waist, and before she had recovered from her shock, I had thrown her in and locked her in my room.
She looked at me, frightened, panicked, terrified, not daring to scream for fear of a scandal, of being undoubtedly chased away by her masters first, and perhaps by her father later.

sentences: He was a professor at the Johannaeum and taught a mineralogy course during which he would regularly get angry once or twice.
Not that he cared about having diligent students in his lessons, nor about the level of attention they paid him, nor about the success they might achieve later; these details hardly worried him.
He taught 'subjectively,' using a term from German philosophy, for himself and not for others.
He was a selfish scholar, a well of knowledge whose pulley creaked when someone tried to draw something from it.
In short, a miser.
There are a few professors of this kind in Germany.
My uncle, unfortunately, did not have an extreme ease of pronunciation, at least not in public, and this is a regrettable flaw for a speaker.

Indeed, during his demonstrations at the Johannaeum, the professor often came to a halt; he struggled with a recalcitrant word that refused to slip between his lips, one of those words that resist, swell, and end up coming out in the unscientific form of an expletive.
Hence, great anger.
In mineralogy, there are many semi-Greek, semi-Latin names that are difficult to pronounce, and these harsh terms would make a poet's lips bleed.
I don't mean to speak ill of this science.
Far from it.

But when faced with rhombohedral crystallizations, retinasphalt resins, ghelénites, tangasites, lead molybdates, manganese tungstates, and zirconium titanates, even the most skilled tongue can trip up.

Now, in the city, people were aware of my uncle's forgivable flaw, and they took advantage of it, waiting for him at tricky moments, which would infuriate him, and they would laugh, which is in poor taste, even for Germans.
So, while there was always a large crowd of listeners at Lidenbrock's lectures, many attended regularly, primarily to enjoy the professor's delightful rages.
In any case, my uncle, I cannot emphasize this enough, was a true scholar.
Although he sometimes broke his samples by testing them too roughly, he combined the genius of a geologist with the eye of a mineralogist.
With his hammer, steel point, magnetic needle, blowtorch, and bottle of nitric acid, he was a very strong man.
At the break, appearance, hardness, fusibility, sound, smell, and taste of any mineral, he would classify it without hesitation among the six hundred species that science recognizes today.

sentences: Tonight is a special evening: it's mom's birthday.
She chose the restaurant: "Chez Giovanni," the Italian restaurant in our neighborhood.
It's her favorite.
The restaurant is small and cozy.
There are photos of Italy on the walls.

We already know the menu by heart.
Mom is having pasta.
Dad is choosing a pizza.
My sister wants lasagna.
And me, a margherita pizza, as always.
At the back of the restaurant, there is a wood-fired oven.
The chef throws the dough in the air.
It's a show!
The dishes are coming.
My pizza smells really good.
I eat everything.
Dad tastes mom's pasta.
"Hey!" says mom.
But she laughs.
In the end, Giovanni arrives with a tiramisu and a candle.
The whole restaurant sings "Happy Birthday!"

sentences: Last month, I had an interview for a part-time job as a waiter in a café.
I had an appointment at two o'clock.
I was nervous.
It was my first interview and I had no experience in a restaurant.
Before leaving, my sister helped me.
"Dress properly, arrive early, and look the person in the eyes."
I arrived at ten to two.
The owner of the café was called Madame Fournier.
She had me sit at a table in the empty café.
She looked at my resume for a few seconds.
It was very short.
"You have never worked in the restaurant business?"
No," I replied.
I wanted to lie a little, but I didn't do it.
"But I learn quickly and I am serious."
She asked other questions.
Could I work on weekends?
Was I available in the evening?
How did I react when a customer was not happy?
This last question was difficult.
I thought for a moment, then I replied: "I would listen first, and I would go get someone if I didn't know what to do."
She nodded slightly.
In the end, she asked me if I had any questions.
I had prepared one: "What is a typical day like here?"
She spoke for five minutes.
Two days later, she called me.
I was starting the following Saturday.

sentences: On Saturday, we visited the city.
We didn't have a specific plan, and it was very nice that way.
We started with the market, in the main square.
It was huge!
There were fruits, cheese, fish, but also clothes and flowers.
We bought strawberries and ate them while walking.
They were delicious.
Then, we entered an old church.
Inside, it was cool and dark.
There was almost nobody.
We sat quietly for ten minutes.
Then we walked through the small streets around the center.
That's where I liked the city the most.
There was laundry in the windows, cats on the walls, and children playing.
It wasn't a tourist area.
In the afternoon, we climbed a hill above the city.
The climb lasted twenty-five minutes and it was hot.
But at the top, the view was beautiful.
You could see the whole city, the river, and the hills behind.
We stayed there for a long time, without talking.
In the evening, we had dinner on the terrace.
My feet hurt: we had walked almost fifteen kilometers.
Before sleeping, my husband said, 'I didn't even know the name of this city a month ago.'
Me neither.
And now, I like it a lot.

sentences: When we think of history, we first think of texts: laws, letters, stories.
However, ordinary objects sometimes tell the past better than official documents.
The reason is simple.
A document is written by someone, with an intention, often by the powerful and for them.
An everyday object, on the other hand, was not made to convey a message.
It testifies unintentionally, and that is precisely what makes it valuable.
A simple pot provides information about what people ate, how they cooked, and what resources they had.
A shoe indicates people's size, their profession, and the distance they traveled.
A coin reveals exchanges, the images that a power wanted to spread, and the extent of trade.
Archaeology is entirely based on this idea.
By digging up material traces, it reconstructs entire societies that left no written records, or whose writings have disappeared.
These objects often correct official narratives.
Ancient texts talk about kings and wars; excavations reveal the lives of peasants, actual diets, diseases, and life expectancy.
Sometimes we discover that daily life was very different from the image presented in the documents.
This is also why what we throw away today will interest historians of tomorrow.
Our waste, our packaging, and our ordinary objects will tell the story of our time more faithfully than our speeches.
An archaeologist put it beautifully.
People lie in their writings.
They rarely lie in their trash.

sentences: Here is a fascinating idea, often misunderstood: the language we speak would influence the way we think.
According to this thesis, the words we have and the distinctions our language imposes would shape even our perception of the world.
Those who speak different languages would not just name the same realities differently: they would, in a sense, see them differently.
This appealing idea deserves to be considered carefully, as it is often both exaggerated and underestimated.
In its strong version, the thesis claims that language would entirely determine thought: one could only conceive what their language allows them to express.
This version is false, and experience disproves it.
We can think of things that our language does not name with a single word; we invent expressions, borrow terms, and forge new concepts.
If language completely imprisoned thought, no new ideas could arise, and translation would be impossible.
Yet we translate, we create, we understand what other languages express differently.
But rejecting the strong version should not lead to denying any influence.
Because in a more modest version, the thesis holds up much better.
Language does not imprison thought, but it guides it, facilitates it here, and slows it down there.
A language that has a precise word for a nuance makes that nuance easier to perceive and handle; a language that requires certain distinctions to be made makes the mind more attentive.
Without trapping us, language traces more or less convenient paths for thought.
Research has highlighted such effects, subtle but real.

According to the categories that their language distinguishes, speakers sometimes show themselves to be quicker to notice certain differences, to remember certain details, and to organize their perception in a certain way.
These effects do not make them prisoners of their language; they only show that it, by slicing the world in its own way, slightly tilts attention and memory.
Language does not dictate thought; it nuances it.
This measured conclusion has implications that go beyond linguistics.
It suggests that speaking multiple languages provides several ways to slice the world, thus, in a sense, enriching one's thinking with multiple perspectives.
It also calls for vigilance: if words shape the mind, then the choice of words in public debate is never innocent.
Naming a reality in a certain way already inclines one to see it that way.
Words do not shape thought on their own, but they do not leave it untouched either.

Between the myth of a language that would determine everything and the illusion of a thought completely independent of words, the truth lies in this middle ground: language is less a prison than a landscape, where some paths are easier than others, but where the mind can always carve out new routes.

sentences: Since any information can now be found in an instant, a question arises: what is the point of memorizing anything at all?
Why remember dates, facts, and knowledge if our phone provides them on demand?
This question, made inevitable by permanent access to knowledge, deserves more than a hasty answer, as it touches on what thought truly is.
The argument in favor of deliberate forgetting seems appealing.
What is the use of burdening your memory with easily accessible data?
Isn't it better to keep the mind free, available for thinking rather than for remembering?
After all, no one regrets not memorizing phone numbers anymore.
Delegating the burden of memorization to machines seems like progress, freeing us for more noble tasks.
This argument, however, overlooks something essential.
Thinking is not about manipulating external information; it requires having integrated knowledge within oneself.
We do not reflect on what we can consult, but on what we know.
To understand a new situation, establish a connection, or have an intuition, knowledge must be present in the mind, ready to combine.
An empty mind, which would need to consult everything, would not think; it would only search.
Memory is not a simple warehouse of information, separate from intelligence.
It is one of its materials.
Ideas arise from the connection of knowledge we possess; creativity itself often consists of linking distant knowledge.
However, we can only connect what we have in mind.
Fully externalizing one's memory would mean depriving oneself of the very material with which we think.
It's not about memorizing everything, nor about considering memorization as an end in itself.
Easy access to information is a real advancement, and freeing the mind from certain burdens is nothing to regret.
But we must distinguish between what we can safely entrust to machines and what must remain within us.
The fundamental knowledge of a field, the kind that allows for understanding and reasoning, cannot be delegated without impoverishing thought itself.
The real question is not about choosing between memorizing and consulting, but about knowing what to keep within ourselves and what to entrust to others.
A mind that would retain nothing would not be a liberated mind; it would be a dispossessed mind, incapable of thinking without support.
Remembering remains, in the age of available information, a condition for thought.

sentences: We spontaneously associate democracy with the power of the majority: what the greatest number decides is democratic.
This equation, seemingly obvious, nonetheless hides a danger that democratic thinkers identified early on: the tyranny of the majority.
For the power of the greatest number, if it is not limited, can oppress minorities and individuals just as surely as a tyrant, in the very name of the democratic principle.
Understanding this danger and the means to guard against it is essential to avoid confusing democracy with the mere law of numbers.
The danger lies in the fact that a majority can, entirely within democratic legality, oppress a minority.

If democracy were reduced to the rule that the majority decides everything, then nothing would prevent this majority from depriving a minority of its rights, persecuting it, and imposing its will without limits.
The legitimacy of numbers does not guarantee the justice of the decision: a majority can want unjust, oppressive, cruel things, and the fact that it is a majority does not make them just.
Reducing democracy to the absolute power of the majority opens the door to oppression that masquerades as legitimacy.
There is something more insidious than legal oppression: the tyranny of the majority can also exert itself on minds, through the pressure of dominant opinion.
In a democratic society, the majority opinion exerts considerable force; it defines what is acceptable to think and say, and places pressure on those who deviate from it to conform.
This tyranny does not operate through law, but through the weight of collective judgment, through the fear of general disapproval, and through the silence it imposes on minority opinions.

It can stifle freedom of thought more effectively than any censorship, as it operates through each individual, in the innermost thoughts of those who no longer dare to stray from what the majority thinks.
How can we protect ourselves from this double tyranny?
The answer has shaped true democracies, which are never reduced to the sheer power of the majority, but are framed by limits.

The first limit is that of fundamental rights, which are exempt from voting: certain things — essential freedoms, the dignity of individuals, the rights of minorities — cannot be abolished by any majority, no matter how large.
These inviolable rights mark a boundary that the majority cannot cross; they protect the individual and the minority from the will of the majority itself.
A democracy is not just the power of the majority; it is the power of the majority limited by rights that escape it.
The second limit relates to the separation of powers and the existence of counter-powers.

In order for a majority not to have absolute power, it is necessary for power to be divided, for independent institutions to provide checks and balances, and for a judiciary to be able to censor unjust decisions, even if they are majority decisions.
These mechanisms, which limit the power of the majority, are not obstacles to democracy, but its conditions: without them, democracy would degenerate into the tyranny of the majority.
A true democracy is a balance between the power of the majority and the limits that prevent it from oppressing.
Recognizing the danger of the tyranny of the majority means understanding that democracy is not just about the rule of numbers, but requires limits that protect against the numbers themselves.
It is to reject the simplistic idea that everything the majority wants is democratic, and to assert that a true democracy protects rights and freedoms against the very will of the majority.
This demand is particularly relevant today, when the legitimacy of numbers is sometimes invoked to justify violations of the rights of minorities or freedoms.

Reminding that the majority does not have all the rights, and that democracy also serves as protection against it, is not anti-democratic: it is defending what distinguishes democracy from mere tyranny of the largest number.

sentences: So, all night long, Lieutenant Hobson and his companions took care of this essential clearing.
Fire and iron kept attacking and breaking down this incoherent mass of ice.
The men handled the pick and the shovel.
The women tended the fires.
Everyone had only one thought: to save Mrs. Paulina Barnett, Madge, Kalumah, Thomas Black!
But when morning returned, these unfortunate people had already been buried for thirty hours, in an air that was necessarily thin beneath the thick layer.
The carpenter, after the work completed during the night, thought about digging the vertical well, which was supposed to lead directly to the roof of the house.
This well, according to his calculations, was not supposed to measure less than fifty feet.

The work would be easy, no doubt, in the ice, that is to say for about twenty feet; but then the difficulties would be great for digging the layer of earth and sand, which was necessarily very loose, and that would need to be supported for at least thirty feet.
Long pieces of wood were therefore prepared for this purpose, and the drilling of the well began.
Only three men could work together there.
The soldiers therefore had the opportunity to take turns often, and it was hoped that the digging would proceed quickly.

The Corsican was walking with a limp.

--Hey!
Nicolas!

sentences: Eating was for a long time one of the simplest acts of existence: we ate what we had, what the region produced, what the season offered.
In just a few decades, this act has strangely become complicated.
Every meal now seems to raise questions: is it good for my health? For the planet? For the animals? For the producers?
What was taken for granted has become a field of concerns and sometimes guilt.
This complexity is not imaginary; it reflects a new reality.

Today we know what we ignored yesterday: the impact of our diet on the climate, the conditions in which animals are raised, the effects of certain products on our bodies, the difficulties of the agricultural world.
This knowledge is a progress, but it has a downside: it burdens every bite with a moral weight that previous generations did not know.
The risk is twofold.
On one hand, a convenient indifference, which consists of wanting to know nothing in order to continue eating without thinking about it.
On the other hand, a constant anxiety, which turns every meal into a dilemma and ultimately spoils a pleasure that is nonetheless essential.
Between blindness and obsession, it is not always easy to find a way.
First, we must recognize that few choices are perfect.
The ideal food — healthy, ecological, ethical, accessible, tasty — almost never exists.
Eating is almost always about navigating contradictory constraints: what is good for health is not always affordable, and what is ecological is not always available.
Demanding perfection is condemning oneself to failure and guilt.
A more reasonable attitude would be to aim for better rather than perfect.
Reduce, without necessarily eliminating; prioritize, without completely forbidding oneself; inform oneself, without becoming paralyzed.
Small changes maintained over time are better than a brief and heroic strictness.
Finally, it is important not to forget what a meal also is: a pleasure, a moment of sharing, a cultural heritage.
By making food too much about calculations and rules, we risk forgetting that it is primarily one of life's great joys.
Eating with awareness, yes; eating with anxiety, certainly not.

sentences: You really put me in a difficult position, I admit, Valentine, by asking what the count has done for me: nothing obvious, I know well.
Also, as I have already told you, my affection for him is entirely instinctive and has nothing rational about it.
Has the sun done anything for me?
No; it warms me, and in its light, I see you, that's all.
Has this or that perfume done anything for me?
No; its scent pleasantly refreshes one of my senses.
I have nothing else to say when asked why I praise this perfume; my friendship for him is as strange as his for me.
A secret voice warns me that there is more than chance in this unexpected and mutual friendship.
I find a correlation even in his simplest actions, even in his most secret thoughts between my actions and my thoughts.
You will laugh at me again, Valentine, but since I have known this man, the absurd idea has come to me that everything good that happens to me comes from him.
However, I lived thirty years without needing this protector, didn't I? Anyway, here’s an example: he invited me to dinner for Saturday, which is natural given where we are, right?
Well, what have I learned since then?
Your father is invited to this dinner, your mother will come.
I will meet with them, and who knows what will come of this meeting in the future?
These circumstances seem very simple at first glance; however, I see something in them that surprises me; I draw a strange confidence from it.

I tell myself that the count, this singular man who guesses everything, wanted me to meet with Mr. and Mrs. de Villefort, and sometimes I try, I swear to you, to read in his eyes if he has guessed my love.

sentences: Florida, discovered by Juan Ponce de León in 1512 on Palm Sunday, was initially named Easter-Flowers.
It hardly deserved this charming name given its arid and scorched coasts.

However, a few miles from the shore, the nature of the land gradually changed, and the country proved worthy of its name; the soil was interspersed with a network of creeks, rivers, streams, ponds, and small lakes; one could have believed they were in Holland or Guiana; but the countryside rose noticeably and soon revealed its cultivated plains, where all the vegetable products from the North and South thrived, its vast fields where the tropical sun and the water retained in the clay of the soil took care of all the cultivation, and finally its pineapple, yam, tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugarcane fields, which stretched as far as the eye could see, displaying their riches with carefree extravagance.
Barbicane appeared very pleased to observe the gradual elevation of the land, and when J.-T. Maston questioned him about it:
"My dear friend," he replied, "we have a primary interest in casting our Columbiad in the highlands.
--To be closer to the Moon?" exclaimed the secretary of the Gun Club.
--No!" Barbicane replied with a smile.
What do a few additional fathoms matter?

No, but in the midst of elevated terrain, our work will proceed more easily; we won't have to contend with water, which will save us from long and costly tubing, and that's something to consider when it comes to drilling a well nine hundred feet deep.

sentences: Well, so what? said Fernand, raising his head and looking at Caderousse, like a man searching for someone to unleash his anger on; Mercédès doesn't depend on anyone, does she? And she's free to love whoever she wants.
Ah! if you take it that way, said Caderousse, that's a different matter!

I thought you were a Catalan; and I was told that Catalans are not the kind of men to let themselves be supplanted by a rival; it was even added that Fernand, in particular, was terrible in his vengeance.
Fernand smiled with pity.
A lover is never terrible, he said.
The poor boy! resumed Danglars, pretending to pity the young man from the bottom of his heart.
What do you want? He didn't expect to see Dantès come back like this all of a sudden; he probably thought he was dead, unfaithful, who knows?
These things are all the more painful when they happen to us all of a sudden.

Ah! indeed, in any case, said Caderousse, who was drinking while speaking and on whom the smoky wine of La Malgue was beginning to take effect, in any case, Fernand is not the only one troubled by Dantès' fortunate return, is he, Danglars?
No, you are right, and I would almost dare to say that this will bring him misfortune.

But never mind, resumed Caderousse, pouring a glass of wine for Fernand, and filling his own glass for the eighth or tenth time while Danglars had barely touched his; never mind, in the meantime, he is marrying Mercédès, the beautiful Mercédès; he's coming back for that, at least.
Meanwhile, Danglars was watching the young man with a piercing gaze, upon whose heart Caderousse's words fell like molten lead.

sentences: Thomas Roch had just escaped, and he was running through the garden, shouting in a voice choked with anger:
"Billions... billions!"
Gaydon then addressed the director, saying:
"I warned you!"

Then he set off in pursuit of his boarder, caught up with him, took him by the arm, and, without encountering much resistance, brought him back to the pavilion, the door of which was immediately closed.
Count d'Artigas remained alone with the director, while Captain Spade made one last tour of the garden along the lower wall.
"I was not exaggerating, sir count," declared the director.
It is clear that Thomas Roch's illness is making new progress every day.
In my opinion, his madness is already incurable.
Even if all the money he asks for were made available to him, nothing could be gained from it...
"That's likely," replied Count d'Artigas, "and yet, even if his financial demands are absurd, he has nonetheless invented a device of virtually infinite power...
That is the opinion of knowledgeable people, my lord.
But what he discovered will soon disappear with him in one of those crises that are becoming more intense and more frequent.
Soon, even the motive of interest, the only one that seems to have survived in his soul, will vanish...
"Perhaps the motive of hatred will remain!" murmured Count d'Artigas, just as Captain Spade was joining him at the garden door.
III Double kidnapping
Half an hour later, Count d'Artigas and Captain Spade were following the path lined with ancient beeches that separates the Healthful-House establishment from the right bank of the Neuze.
Both had taken leave of the director, who said he was very honored by their visit, while they thanked him for his kind welcome.
A hundred dollars, intended for the staff of the house, testified to Count d'Artigas's generous disposition.
It was, how could one doubt it?
a foreigner of the highest distinction, if distinction is measured by generosity.
