sentences: The professor finally emerged from his cabin, a bit pale, somewhat defeated, but still enthusiastic, with a look of satisfaction in his eyes.
The townspeople, particularly interested in the arrival of a ship from which everyone had something to gain, gathered on the quay.
My uncle was eager to leave his floating prison, not to mention his hospital.

But before leaving the deck of the schooner, he led me to the front, and there, pointing with his finger, he showed me a tall mountain with two peaks, a double cone covered in eternal snow, located in the northern part of the bay.
"The Sneffels!" he exclaimed, "the Sneffels!"
Then, after gesturing for me to remain absolutely silent, he got into the waiting boat.
I followed him, and soon we were setting foot on the soil of Iceland.
At first, a well-built man appeared, dressed in a general's uniform.
However, he was just a simple magistrate, the governor of the island, Baron Trampe himself.
The professor recognized who he was dealing with.
He handed the governor his letters from Copenhagen, and a brief conversation in Danish ensued, to which I remained completely foreign, and for good reason.
But from this first meeting, it resulted that Baron Trampe was entirely at the disposal of Professor Lidenbrock.
My uncle received a very warm welcome from the mayor, Mr. Finson, who was just as military in his attire as the governor, but also peaceful by nature and position.
As for the coadjutor, Mr. Pictursson, he was currently on an episcopal tour in the Northern Bailiwick; we would have to temporarily give up being introduced to him.
But a charming man, whose assistance became very valuable to us, was Mr. Fridriksson, a professor of natural sciences at the school in Reykjavik.
This modest scholar spoke only Icelandic and Latin; he came to offer me his services in the language of Horace, and I felt that we were meant to understand each other.
Indeed, he was the only person I could converse with during my stay in Iceland.

sentences: Then suddenly, in this wonderful nature, he experienced a complete and sudden regeneration: he got up, leaped out of the room, and rushed down the stairs, shouting at the top of his lungs:
Julie!
Julie!
Emmanuel!
Emmanuel!
Monte-Cristo wanted to rush out as well, but Maximilien would rather have been killed than leave the door frame that he was pushing against the count.
At Maximilien's cries, Julie, Emmanuel, Peneton, and a few servants rushed in, terrified.
Morrel took them by the hands, and reopening the door:
"Kneel!" he cried in a voice choked with sobs; "kneel! it's the benefactor, it's the savior of our father! it's..."
He was about to say:
"It's Edmond Dantès!"
The count stopped him by grabbing his arm.
Julie leaped onto the count's hand; Emmanuel embraced her like a protective god; Morrel fell to his knees for the second time and struck the floor with his forehead.
Then the man of bronze felt his heart swell in his chest, a jet of consuming flame shot from his throat to his eyes, he bowed his head and wept!
In that room, for a few moments, there was a concert of sublime tears and moans that must have sounded harmonious even to the most cherished angels of the Lord!

Julie had barely recovered from the deep emotion she had just experienced when she dashed out of the room, went down a floor, ran to the living room with childlike joy, and lifted the crystal globe that protected the purse given by the stranger from the Allées de Meilhan.
Meanwhile, Emmanuel was saying to the count in a broken voice:

sentences: This time, Danglars understood doubly: he understood through words and gestures, for the man walking behind him pushed him so roughly forward that he bumped into his guide.
This guide was our friend Peppino, who plunged into the tall grass through a winding path that only weasels and lizards could recognize as a beaten track.

Peppino stopped in front of a rock topped with a thick bush; this rock, slightly open like an eyelid, allowed passage to the young man, who disappeared into it like the devils of our fairy tales vanish into their traps.
The voice and gesture of the one following Danglars prompted the banker to do the same.
There was no longer any doubt, the French bankrupt was dealing with Roman bandits.
Danglars complied like a man caught between two terrible dangers, and whom fear makes brave.
Despite his stomach being in no condition to navigate the crevices of the Roman countryside, he slipped in behind Peppino, and, closing his eyes as he let himself slide, he landed on his feet.
Upon touching the ground, he opened his eyes again.
The path was wide, but dark.
Peppino, not concerned about hiding now that he was home, struck a match and lit a torch.
Two other men descended behind Danglars, forming the rear guard, and, pushing Danglars whenever he happened to stop, guided him down a gentle slope to the center of a sinister-looking crossroads.
Indeed, the walls, carved into stacked coffins, seemed, amidst the white stones, to open those black and deep eyes one notices in skulls.
A sentry struck the cap of his rifle against his left hand.
"Who goes there?" asked the sentry.
"Friend, friend!" said Peppino.
Where is the captain?
"There," said the sentry, pointing over his shoulder to a large hall carved into the rock, the light of which reflected into the corridor through large arched openings.
"Good prey, captain, good prey," said Peppino in Italian.
And taking Danglars by the collar of his coat, he led him to an opening that resembled a door, through which one could enter the hall that the captain seemed to have made his quarters.

sentences: Sir, said the inspector, Providence has fortunately brought some change to this gigantic plan of which you seem to be quite an enthusiastic supporter.
It's the only way to make Italy a strong, independent, and happy state, replied the abbé.

That is possible, replied the inspector, but I didn't come here to give you a lesson in ultramontane politics; I came to ask you what I've already done, if you have any complaints about how you are fed and housed.
The food is what it is in all prisons, replied the abbé, that is to say, very bad; as for the accommodation, you can see it is damp and unhealthy, but still quite suitable for a dungeon.
Now, that's not what this is about, but rather revelations of the utmost importance and interest that I have to make to the government.
Here we are, said the governor quietly to the inspector.
That's why I'm so happy to see you, continued the abbé, although you have interrupted me in a very important calculation, which, if successful, might change Newton's system.
Can you grant me the favor of a private meeting?
Huh! what was I saying! said the governor to the inspector.
You know your worth, replied the latter with a smile.
Then, turning to Faria:
Sir, he said, what you are asking me is impossible.
However, sir, the abbé replied, if it were a matter of making the government a huge sum, say five million, for example?
Indeed, said the inspector, turning back to the governor, you even predicted the amount.
Come now, the abbé replied, noticing that the inspector was making a move to leave, it is not necessary for us to be completely alone; Mr. Governor can attend our conversation.
My dear sir, the governor said, unfortunately we already know by heart what you will say.
It's about your treasures, isn't it?
Faria looked at this mocking man with eyes where an impartial observer would certainly have seen the spark of reason and truth.
Of course, he said; what do you want me to talk about, if not that?
Mr. Inspector, the governor continued, I can tell you this story just as well as the abbé, because I have been hearing about it for four or five years.

sentences: Danglars turned towards the left door.
Another man on horseback was galloping to the left door.
"Indeed, Danglars thought, sweat on his brow, indeed I am caught."
And he sank back into the depths of his carriage, this time not to sleep, but to think.
A moment later, the moon rose.

From the back of the carriage, he cast his gaze into the countryside; he then saw again those great aqueducts, stone phantoms, that he had noticed while passing; only, instead of having them on his right, he now had them on his left.
He understood that they had turned the carriage around and were bringing him back to Rome.
"Oh! unfortunate man, he murmured, they must have obtained the extradition!"
The carriage continued to run at a frightening speed.
An hour passed terribly, for with each new clue thrown in his path, the fugitive recognized, without a doubt, that they were bringing him back.
Finally, he saw a dark mass against which it seemed the carriage was going to collide.
But the carriage swerved, passing alongside this dark mass, which was none other than the belt of walls that surrounds Rome.
Oh! oh! murmured Danglars, we're not going back into the city, so it's not justice that's stopping me.
Good God! another idea, could it be...?
His hair stood on end.

He remembered those interesting stories about Roman bandits, so little believed in Paris, which Albert de Morcerf had told to Mrs. Danglars and Eugénie when it was a question of the young viscount becoming the son of one and the husband of the other.
Thieves, perhaps! he murmured.
Suddenly the carriage rolled over something harder than the ground of a sandy road.

Danglars took a glance to both sides of the road; he spotted strange-shaped monuments, and his mind, preoccupied with Morcerf's tale, which was now presenting itself to him in all its details, told him that he must be on the Appian Way.
To the left of the carriage, in a sort of valley, there was a circular excavation.
It was the circus of Caracalla.
At a word from the man galloping at the right door, the carriage stopped.

sentences: The next day, July 5th, around three o'clock in the afternoon, the detachment finally stopped at the tip of Cape Bathurst.
It remained to determine the exact position of this cape, which the maps placed above the seventieth parallel.
But one could not rely on the hydrographic survey of these coasts, which had not yet been done with sufficient precision.
In the meantime, Jasper Hobson decided to stop in this place.
"What is stopping us from settling here permanently?" asked Corporal Joliffe.
You will agree, my lieutenant, that the place is appealing.
"It will certainly appeal to you even more," replied Lieutenant Hobson, "if you receive double pay for it, my worthy corporal."
"That is not in doubt," replied Corporal Joliffe, "and we must comply with the Company's instructions."
"So wait until tomorrow," added Jasper Hobson, "and if, as I suspect, this Cape Bathurst is indeed located beyond the seventieth degree of northern latitude, we will pitch our tent there."
The location was indeed favorable for establishing a trading post.
The shores of the lagoon, lined with wooded hills, could abundantly provide the pines, birches, and other types of wood necessary for the construction and heating of the new fort.
The lieutenant, having advanced with a few of his companions to the very tip of the cape, noted that to the west, the coast curved in a very elongated arc.
Fairly high cliffs closed off the horizon a few miles beyond.
As for the waters of the lagoon, it was recognized that they were fresh and not brackish as one might have thought, due to the proximity of the sea.

However, in any case, fresh water would not have been lacking for the colony, even if these waters had been undrinkable, because a small river, then clear and cool, flowed towards the icy Ocean and emptied into it through a narrow mouth, a few hundred steps southeast of Cape Bathurst.

This mouth, protected not by rocks but by a rather unusual accumulation of earth and sand, formed a natural harbor, in which two or three ships would have been perfectly sheltered from the open sea winds.
This arrangement could be advantageously used for the anchoring of vessels that would later come from the Bering Strait.
Jasper Hobson, out of gallantry towards the traveler, named this small stream Paulinariver, and the small harbor Port-Barnett, which delighted the traveler.

sentences: Oppose me, sir, replied Michel Ardan with perfect gallantry, oppose as much as you like!
You know, said the stranger, that when light rays pass through a medium like air, they are deflected from a straight line, or, in other words, they undergo refraction.
Well! when stars are obscured by the Moon, their rays, grazing the edges of the disk, have never experienced the slightest deflection nor given the faintest hint of refraction.
From this, it follows that the Moon is not surrounded by an atmosphere.
They looked at the Frenchman, for once the observation was accepted, the consequences were rigorous.

Indeed, replied Michel Ardan, that is your best argument, if not your only one, and a scholar might be hard-pressed to respond to it; I will only tell you that this argument does not have absolute value, because it assumes the angular diameter of the Moon is perfectly determined, which it is not.
But let's move on, and tell me, my dear sir, if you accept the existence of volcanoes on the surface of the Moon.
Extinct volcanoes, yes; active ones, no.
Let me believe, however, and without exceeding the bounds of logic, that these volcanoes were active for a certain period!
That is certain, but since they could provide the necessary oxygen for combustion themselves, the fact of their eruption does not prove the presence of a lunar atmosphere at all.
Let's move on then, replied Michel Ardan, and set aside this kind of argument to get to direct observations.
But I warn you that I am going to put some names forward.
Put.
I put.
In 1715, astronomers Louville and Halley, observing the eclipse of May 3rd, noticed some strange flashes of a peculiar nature.
These bursts of light, quick and often renewed, were attributed by them to storms raging in the atmosphere of the Moon.
--In 1715, replied the unknown, astronomers Louville and Halley mistook purely terrestrial phenomena, such as meteors or others, for lunar phenomena occurring in our atmosphere.
This is what the scholars responded to the statement of these facts, and this is what I respond along with them.
--Let's move on, replied Ardan, undisturbed by the retort.
Did Herschell, in 1787, not observe a large number of bright spots on the surface of the Moon?

sentences: In January, in France, people eat the galette des rois.
It's a very popular tradition.
The galette is a round and golden cake.
Inside, there is almond cream.
But the galette has a secret.
In the cake, there is a fève, a small figure.
The person who finds the fève becomes the king or the queen.
She puts on a paper crown.
On Sunday, the whole family is at our house.
The youngest child goes under the table.
Mom cuts a piece and asks, 'For whom?'
The child under the table gives a name.
That way, no one cheats!
This year, it's my little brother Léo who is under the table.
Everyone laughs.
Everyone eats their piece slowly.
Watch out for your teeth, the fève is hard!
Suddenly, Léo shouts, "I have something!"
It's the fève!
Léo is the king.
He puts on the crown.
It's too big, but he is very proud.
Long live King Léo, and long live the galette!
It all started with a comment from my daughter Camille, who is eight years old, during an ecology lesson: "Dad, why do we throw the peels in the trash?
The teacher says we can make compost."
Good question.
I didn't have a good answer.
So, last year, we started.
I set up a compost bin at the back of the garden.
Honestly, I had doubts: I imagined terrible smells.
The rule is simple.
In the compost, we put peels, coffee grounds, eggshells, and dry leaves.
We don't put meat, fish, or cheese.
Camille is the compost boss and empties the small bucket every evening.
And what about bad smells?
Surprise: there aren't any.
A well-made compost smells like the forest, not the trash.
The secret is the mix, and you need to stir it from time to time.
In the bin, an invisible army is at work: earthworms, insects, and microscopic fungi.
Camille calls them 'our little workers.'
After several months, the magic was there: beautiful black, soft, and rich soil.
Gardeners call it 'black gold.'
In the spring, we gave it to our tomatoes.
The result: delicious tomatoes, and a trash can that shrank by a third!
Our peels feed the garden, and the garden feeds us.
The loop is complete, as Camille's teacher says.

sentences: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
You know the saying; your parents already knew it.
It has the solidity of a proverb and the authority of a law.
A little awkward question: where does it come from?
Partly... from advertisements by cereal manufacturers in the early twentieth century.
The most effective slogans end up sounding like science.
That doesn't mean the saying is false — but it invites us to take a closer look.
What does research say, exactly?
More nuanced things than the proverb.
Yes, a good breakfast has real benefits, especially for certain people.
After a night of fasting, the body and the brain appreciate an energy intake.
For children and teenagers, studies are quite clear: those who have breakfast in the morning concentrate better in class during the morning.
For a schoolchild, skipping breakfast is rarely a good idea.
But for adults, the obligation doesn't hold.
Contrary to a common belief, skipping breakfast doesn't make you gain weight and doesn't 'block' the metabolism: serious studies have found no catastrophic effects.
Millions of people simply aren't hungry in the morning, and forcing them to eat makes no sense.
The body generally knows what it's doing.
The real rule is disappointingly simple: if you're hungry in the morning, eat; if not, don't.
The most interesting question is not actually, "Should we have breakfast?" but rather, "What should we put on our plate?"
Because not all breakfasts are equal, and the most common one is probably the worst: sugary cereals, fruit juice, white bread, and jam.
A meal almost entirely made up of sugar.
It causes a quick energy spike... followed by a drop just as fast.
It's the famous "10:30 slump," with cravings and a lack of focus.
Your sugary breakfast has betrayed you.
The solution is well-known: proteins and fibers.
An egg, plain yogurt, cheese, whole grain bread, a handful of nuts, a whole fruit instead of juice.
This type of meal releases its energy slowly and keeps you going until lunch, without the rollercoaster effect.
So, is it the most important meal of the day?
Let's say instead: a meal like any other — neither sacred nor mandatory, but deserving of better than sugary, colorful boxes.
The most important thing, after all, might simply be to start the day without lying to yourself about what's in the bowl.

sentences: I'm too old to learn a language.
This is one of the most common beliefs, and one of the most false.
It is based on an accurate observation, but misinterpreted.
It is true that children acquire a perfect accent more easily, and that a young brain absorbs certain things effortlessly.
But the accent is just a small part of a language, and the rest often benefits adults.
An adult understands structures, makes connections with what they already know, and learns through logic as much as through imitation.
They choose their methods and know why they are learning.
These advantages largely compensate for a memory that is a bit less flexible.
What really changes is not the abilities, but the conditions.
An adult has less time, more fatigue, and especially much more fear of ridicule.
It is this last point, much more than age, that holds back most people.
Learning a language forces you to do something unpleasant: speak poorly, for a long time, in front of others.
You have to accept looking like a child, searching for your words, and making mistakes.
Adults hate this, precisely because they are used to being competent.
But this is exactly where success lies.
Those who make progress are not the most talented: they are the ones who accept being bad for a long time.
The benefits, on the other hand, go beyond the language itself.
Traveling differently, accessing a culture from the inside, and, according to some studies, keeping your brain active.
So it is never too late.
The only real question is not 'Am I capable of it?'
It is: 'Am I ready to make mistakes for a year?'

sentences: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.

This statement from a philosopher, as famous as it is enigmatic, exerts a lasting fascination on the mind, as it touches on one of the most dizzying questions there is: the relationship between language and thought, between what we can say and what we can think, conceive, and feel.
Should we understand it as the assertion that nothing exists for us beyond what our language allows us to express?
Or does it say something more subtle, which does not confine thought to words, but indicates a more fluid boundary?
To probe this statement is to question the powers and servitudes of language.

Taken in its strongest sense, the statement would assert that our world is reduced to what our language can say, that the unspeakable does not exist for us, that to think is to speak inwardly, and that beyond words there is nothing.

This thesis has a certain power, as it accounts for the hold of language on our experience: we think in words, we articulate the world according to the categories of our language, and what we cannot name often eludes us.
A language rich in distinctions allows us to perceive nuances that a poorer language leaves indistinct; the vocabulary we have shapes, in a sense, the world we inhabit.
In this regard, there is indeed a truth in the idea that our language shapes our world.

However, taken literally, this thesis encounters decisive objections, first and foremost this one: we constantly experience that thought exceeds language, that we conceive more than we can say, and that experience surpasses the words we have for it.
Who hasn't experienced this powerlessness of language, searching in vain for the words for an emotion, an intuition, or a nuance that resists expression?
If our world were limited to the confines of our language, this experience of the unspeakable would be impossible; yet it is universal.
The very feeling that words are lacking proves that we are reaching something that exceeds words, that thought touches upon what language cannot grasp.
Thought is therefore not imprisoned by language; it overflows it, it precedes it, and it tests its limits from within.
Moreover.
If thought were strictly confined by existing language, how could language itself enrich itself?
Yet we forge new words, we invent expressions, we expand our language precisely to say what it did not yet express.
This linguistic creation assumes that we first conceive what we cannot yet name, that thought precedes the word it calls for.
Language does not always precede thought; it sometimes follows it, trying to catch up with what it has already glimpsed.
This precedence of thought over words, in the act of creation, contradicts the idea that language would absolutely limit what can be thought.
Should we then reverse the formula and assert that thought would be entirely free with respect to language, which would be nothing more than an external garment?
That would be to fall into the opposite excess, equally false.
For while it is true that thought exceeds language, it is also true that language structures it, nourishes it, and makes it possible.
We do not think in a pure ether, independently of any language; our concepts, our distinctions, our reasoning are largely woven from words.
A thought without language would be formless, fleeting, incapable of fixing itself, developing, or being transmitted.
Language does not imprison thought, but carries it, and without it, thought would hardly be more than an inarticulate tremor.
Truth may lie in this irreducible tension: thought exceeds language, and yet it depends on it; language limits it, and yet it surpasses it.
The boundaries of my language are not the walls of a prison where my thought would be confined, but rather the shifting shore where it encounters what it cannot yet express and strives to conquer.

Learning a language, in this sense, is not just about acquiring words; it is about expanding the boundaries of one's world, gaining new nuances, new perceptions, and new ways of articulating experience.

Each new language is another world, and those who possess several inhabit a broader world—not that their thought was imprisoned, but because each language offers them new means to express what they perhaps already sensed without being able to articulate it.

sentences: For a long time, I went to bed late and woke up tired, without ever really worrying about it.
I thought that this fatigue was normal, simply the price to pay for a busy professional life.
Many people around me seemed to be experiencing the same thing, which reassured me, in a way.
One day, during a routine medical check-up, my doctor asked me a simple question: 'How many hours do you sleep on average?'
I answered, almost proudly, 'About five hours, but I'm doing just fine.'
His look made me realize that my answer wasn't as reassuring as I thought.
He calmly explained to me that this chronic lack of sleep was probably affecting much more than I imagined: my concentration, my mood, my long-term health.
This conversation made me seriously reflect, for the first time, on my sleeping habits.
I realized that I had normalized something that, in reality, was not normal at all.
By talking about it with those around me, I discovered that several colleagues were living exactly the same situation, without ever really questioning it themselves either.
This shared discovery reassured me a bit, while confirming how widespread this denial of sleep deprivation seems to be in my professional circle.
Since that day, I've been trying, with varying success, to go to bed earlier.
It's not perfect yet, but at least I no longer see my constant fatigue as an unavoidable fate.

sentences: --The other one, the abbé continued without seeming to notice Caderousse's emotion, was named Danglars; the third one, he added, although my rival, loved me too.
A devilish smile lit up Caderousse's features as he made a move to interrupt the abbé.
"Wait, said the abbé, let me finish, and if you have any comments to make, you can do so later.
"The other one, although my rival, loved me too and was named Fernand; as for my fiancée, her name was..."
I can't remember the name of my fiancée, said the abbé.
--Mercédès, said Caderousse.

sentences: Moreover, Rodolphe added, perhaps, from the world's perspective, one is right?
How so? she asked.
Well, don't you know that there are souls who are constantly tormented?
They need both dreams and action in turn, the purest passions, the wildest pleasures, and thus one throws oneself into all sorts of fantasies and madness.
Then she looked at him as one looks at a traveler who has passed through extraordinary lands, and she replied:
We poor women don't even have that distraction!
A sad distraction because one doesn't find happiness in it.
But do we ever find it? she asked.
Yes, it is encountered one day, he replied.
"And this is what you have understood, said the Counselor.

You, farmers and workers of the countryside; you, peaceful pioneers of a work entirely of civilization! you, men of progress and morality! you have understood, I say, that political storms are indeed more fearsome than the disorders of the atmosphere..."
One day, he said again, all of a sudden, when one had lost hope.
Then horizons open up, it’s like a voice that cries out: 'There it is!'
You feel the need to share the secrets of your life with this person; to give them everything, to sacrifice everything for them!
You can't explain it, you just sense it.
You have glimpsed each other in your dreams.
(And he was looking at her.) Finally, there it is, that treasure you have searched for so long, right in front of you; it shines, it sparkles.
Yet you still doubt it, you don't dare to believe it; you remain dazzled, as if you were emerging from darkness into light.
And as he finished these words, Rodolphe added a pantomime to his statement.
He ran his hand over his face, like a man who is dizzy; then he let it fall onto Emma's.
She withdrew hers.
But the Counselor was still reading:
And who would be surprised by that, gentlemen?
Only someone who would be blind enough, deeply immersed (I don't hesitate to say), deeply immersed in the prejudices of another age to still misunderstand the spirit of agricultural populations.
Where indeed can one find more patriotism than in the countryside, more dedication to the public cause, more intelligence in a word?

And I do not mean, gentlemen, this superficial intelligence, a vain ornament of idle minds, but rather this deep and moderate intelligence, which applies above all to pursue useful goals, thereby contributing to the good of each, to the common improvement, and to the support of the States, the fruit of respect for the laws and the practice of duties...
